Excavation Licence No. 04E0039
This licence was issued in respect of features exposed during a monitored topsoil-strip over the area of a borrow pit adjacent to the route of the N11 Ashford-Rathnew bypass. Agreement was reached between the developer and the National Monuments Service that these features could be preserved in situ, covered with geotextile and sand prior to the total reinstatement of the field, having been lightly cleaned, planned and recorded.  The features, in the main, would appear to represent aspects of a severely truncated prehistoric landscape. The most substantial remains are the traces of a subcircular foundation trench, 4.9m by 5m in diameter. The trench is likely to be quite shallow, given the level of truncation over this area as a result of deep ploughing. This feature would appear to represent the remains of a small, prehistoric house. The other features are far more ephemeral in nature, being largely small, amorphous spreads and deposits and occasional areas of localised burning. The absence of any diagnostic material from the site renders it difficult to date the activity (Bennett 2007, 475-6).

Date of upload:  30 October 2012

Excavation licence Number 02E0701
Excavation took place between 20 May and 11 June 2002. The site appeared as a small area of raised ground adjacent to a small south-running stream and an area of flat marshland that surrounds the stream and borders the site to the west. To the east is a steeply sloping hill that rises to a height of over 90m. Ground clearing revealed the remnants of a fulacht fiadh or burnt mound. Excavation of a portion of the mound and two associated troughs followed. There were no finds from the site that would indicate a period of occupation, although fulachta fiadh are usually dated to the Bronze Age (Bennett 2007, 476). 

Editor's note: Though carried out in 2002, this summary was received too late for inclusion in the bulletin of that year.

This stone was found in 1908 by a group of men hunting ferrets near Hollywood, Co. Wicklow.  It was lying face down at the edge of a grassy lane at Lockstown Upper (WI016-017----). It consists of a boulder (dims. c. 1.2m by 0.9m and 0.8m thick) carved with a labyrinth design (diam. c. 0.7m). A small section of the labyrinth is missing where a section was broken from the stone: this had been done prior to its discovery.  The labyrinth appears to have been carved using the classical seed pattern and it is not known which way the labyrinth was intended to be viewed though it seems probable that it may been positioned so that its opening was at the bottom. The exact purpose of this stone is unknown though it seems likely that it had some connection with the pilgrimage to Glendalough and may have been used as a marker or station along the route where pilgrims stopped to pray. The labyrinth design has been replicated as a landscape feature in front of the Visitor Centre. (Orpen 1911; Price and Walshe 1933, 48)

Twenty cross slabs (WI042-019006-/033-) can be seen scattered about Aghowle graveyard (WI042-019003-), all of which have been reused as upright burial markers, which largely explains the main distribution of the cross slabs in the southern part of the graveyard, coinciding with the main area of 18th and 19th century headstones. It is clear that the majority of the cross slabs were originally intended as recumbent slabs, however, their current use as upright headstones means that most of the slabs are partially concealed, thereby limiting the visible features. The majority are schist slabs, except for Cross slabs 2, 11, 15 and 16 which are of granite (Corlett 2019).  
Described by Corlett (2019) as following; 'Cross slab 12 is situated c. 10m south of the west doorway of Aghowle Church (WI042-019001-). The granite slab is 9cm thick and presently stands 44cm high. The slab is 50cm wide at the base and tapers slightly to 42cm wide at the top. On the east face is an outline Latin cross 33cm across. The terminal of upper transom is slightly damaged where the top of the stone has shattered. The lower transom continues below the ground surface. The cross is formed by a shallow groove (2cm across, 8mm deep)'.

Immediately east of St Finden’s Cross (WI042-019002-) is a large block of granite (L 1.3m; Wth 0.73m; H 0.43m) which originally stood much higher. It is unshaped, except along one side which has been given quite a flat face – notably the rim is lower along this side of the stone. The basin is trough-like (L 0.84m; Wth 0.47m; D 0.55m) and the upper sides are straight, but the lower sides, including the ends, slope gradually towards a narrow base, providing a V-shaped profile across the short-axis. There is no drain hole. Given the lack of drain hole, the basin is rarely without water, and according to John O’Donovan “the water ... is believed to be blessed and able to cure headaches etc, for as the stone retains the blessing of St. Fenden, it imparts it to every drop of rain water which falls into it” (OSL).

Fourteen archaeological features/deposits were uncovered during test excavation under licence no. 06E0273 in Glebe townland, Co. Wicklow. The test excavation was undertaken in advance of a proposed housing development at the site. The deposit types identified in the assessment consisted of ditches (field enclosures dating from between ad 1000 and 1800) and 18th-century brick-manufacturing deposits.
The most interesting discovery was the identification of a substantial hearth within a rectangular house foundation in Trench 13. A rectangular ‘church’ building is illustrated on the first-edition of the OS as ‘site of the church of Drumkay’ (WI025-011----) in this location. Other features and deposits such as pits, a possible corn-drying kiln and the foundations of a masonry wall were also identified throughout the remainder of the site. There was no definitive evidence to suggest that the features identified in the separate trenches were contemporary. Archaeological deposits similar to those described above were also uncovered in an assessment carried out by William O. Frazer close to the site (Excavations 2002, No. 1993, 02E0226). Significantly, no characteristic church-type deposits, burials, church masonry or ecclesiastical structural remains were found in the test-trenches.
The testing demonstrated that the church of Drumkay was not located within the RMP constraint circle, although a ‘building’ with a hearth was discovered within the constraint circle. It is clear from the OS mapping that this structure was no longer standing in 1837, although the foundations must have been visible and recorded in error as the church site. These findings suggest that either the church site of Drumkay is located beyond the current test-trench locations, or that the nature of the recorded monument is not consistent with a typical church site.
Postscript: Subsequent to the testing on this site, archaeological excavations in a neighbouring part of Glebe townland uncovered the church and graveyard (WI025-011006-) of Drumkay (Bennett 2009, 574-5).

A ring-ditch (WI013-077----), a large cremation pit (WI013-113----) and two small structures (WI013-114----and WI013-115----) were excavated here in 2003, prior to the construction of the dual carriageway from the R671 to Greystones (Excavation Licence 03E0147 (Site F)). The ring-ditch (Wth 1.4m; av. D 0.6m) enclosed a circular area (diams. 5.6m N-S; 5.39m E-W). Nine flints were found in the ditch. The cremation pit was located 3.07m to the north-east of the ring-ditch and contained deposits of cremated bone, charcoal and large stones. A small circular structure (diam. 3m N-S; 2.8m E-W), 10m to the west of the ring-ditch, was defined by a narrow, circular slot-trench with two post-holes defining an entrance (Wth 0.9m). There was also a centrally placed post-hole and the slot-trench was ringed with an outer circle of post-holes in which several fragments of prehistoric pottery were found. A second, small structure, located 11m north of the former, was formed by a series of post-holes and stake-holes which defined a circular depression (diam. 2.76m; D 0.14m). (Molloy 2006, 546)

In 1993 a geophysical survey was carried out by Geoquest Associates of Durham, England under licence No. 93E0187 in the field containing St. Crispin's Cell (WI008-012001-) and in the field to the W of the church. Magnetometer and selective resistivity survey of the west field indicated a relatively featureless geophysical terrain. Five small areas had positive magnetic lines which were interpreted as possible shallow ditches. Work in the east field revealed a series of features, possibly shallow ditches, most pronounced in a 40m x 40m area north-west of the church. Excavation was undertaken by Charles Mount in 1993 under licence No. 93E0187.  The excavation examined the south-western corner of the east field and the “hollow way” (WI008-072----) which runs in a north–south direction across the western end of this field.
Cutting 14 examined the hollow way. It measured 20m x 1m and was excavated to 1.03m in depth. The stratigraphy consisted of the sod layer which in the position of the hollow way was compressed to only 0.4m in thickness. This overlay a dark brown soil. In the area of the hollow this overlay a stone layer 0.3m in thickness and 3.2m in width. On the western side it abutted the lighter coloured subsoil but on the east it petered out. The surface hollow was not centred on this stone layer as the former’s western edge was nearly in the base of the feature.
Flint was most frequent and accounted for 85 finds. It occurred across the site but entirely in the sod and topsoil. Forty-six percent of the flints were unstruck pebbles, 25% were flakes, 16% were chipped cores and pebbles and 9% were scrapers. The high percentage of unchipped pebbles and chipped pebbles and cores, 62%, in comparison to the low percentage of scrapers, 9%, and their poor quality, suggests that this was a site at which flint pebbles were collected from the nearby shore and were made into artefacts. Pottery, at 29% of the finds, was mostly composed of 19th-century wares. Glazed red wares of possible medieval to 18th century date were scarce and unglazed red ware, of possible early medieval or prehistoric date, were scarcer again. Animal bone accounted for 11% of the finds and iron 7%.
Excavation confirmed Halpin’s interpretation that the earliest feature in this area was a ditch, subsequently filled in and used as a routeway. Two sherds of glazed medieval pottery and a sherd of medieval cooking ware were recovered from the upper fills of the ditch but no diagnostic finds were made in the primary fills so the date of the feature remains unknown (Eogan and O'Brien 2005)

On a S facing slope on the crest of a ridge in forestry, with good views to the S towards Ballinacor. A small drystone cairn (diam. 2.5m; H 0.4m) containing a large number of quartz stones with traces of a bank (Wth 1.8m; H 0.4m) forming an arc from NE to SSE (est. diam. 10m) with possible W half cut by forest track. A large stone has been set upright on top of the cairn in recent times.  
In 1935 Charles MacNeill recorded that the site was known as Art O’Neill’s Cairn (Corlett and Weaver 2002, vol 1, 271-2), from the tradition that it marked the grave of Art O’Neill, who died on his way to Glenmalure in January 1592 having escaped from Dublin Castle, in the company of Red Hugh O’Donnell. It is generally believed however that the place known as Art’s Cross in Oakwood in west Wicklow is the true location of Art O’Neil’s grave. MacNeill also noted in 1935 that this site was known locally as ‘the Cloran' (ibid), and it is possible that the name derives from ceallúrnán, meaning small burial ground.

Located in the E quadrant of Ballintemple graveyard (WI040-011003-).   Window sill of medieval church (WI040-011002-) set upright and appears to have been reused as a headstone which is decorated with prehistoric cup marks. The stone consists of a shale pillar-like stone (L 0.75m; Wth 0.29m; T 0.09m) with one end of the stone decorated with a series of cupmarks on both faces. On one face are nine cup marks ranging from 2cm to 5cm across and 0.5cm to 2.5cm deep; the largest of these appears to cut the edge of a small cup. One edge of the stone has been broken away so that two of the cups are now on the edge of the stone and only survive partially. Notably, these two cups appear to have met a pair of cupmarks on the opposite face. On this face are seven cups. It is also notable that two of the other cups appear to be directly opposite cupmarks on the other face. In one corner a hole extends through the thickness of the stone. It appears that this was formed where cupmarks on either side have met and broken through the thickness of the stone. The stone was clearly reused afterwards as a window sill; the plunging internal and external bases of the window have been finely carved near the centre of the stone. This window was some 31.5cm wide. The external splay measures 43cm across (Corlett 2013, 14-15).

Twenty cross slabs (WI042-019006-/033-) can be seen scattered about Aghowle graveyard (WI042-019003-), all of which have been reused as upright burial markers, which largely explains the main distribution of the cross slabs in the southern part of the graveyard, coinciding with the main area of 18th and 19th century headstones. It is clear that the majority of the cross slabs were originally intended as recumbent slabs, however, their current use as upright headstones means that most of the slabs are partially concealed, thereby limiting the visible features. The majority are schist slabs, except for Cross slabs 2, 11, 15 and 16 which are of granite (Corlett 2019).  
Described by Corlett (2019) as following; 'Cross slab 15 is situated in the western quadrant of Aghowle graveyard (WI042-019003-). It has been reused as a headstone and is firmly embedded in the ground, so that only the top portion is visible above the ground. The granite slab measures 24.5cm wide and 8cm thick, and features an incised cross on the east face. The upper transom is 9cm wide. Only the incised lines forming the upper portion of the arms are visible and extend the full width of the slab. The underside of the arms and the shaft are concealed below the ground surface'.

The rectangular granite stone measures 83cm x 37cm across. The stone is crudely shaped. It is well-embedded in the ground and may be in situ, though it is leaning to the east, so that this side of the stone is concealed beneath the ground. However, this also means that a large portion of the west side is exposed, and features an incised rectangular frame (36cm wide, 25cm high) enclosing twelve square bosses, arranged in three

On the top surface is a circular socket (13cm across and 11cm deep) with a rounded or bowl-shaped base. At first glance this resembles a mortar, but it probably represents a socket. This monument is subject to a preservation order made under the National Monuments Acts 1930 to 2014 (PO no. 127/1940).

On the steep westernmost slope of Lugnagun ridge. A cairn (WI005-058---) is located on the summit of the ridge, at the eastern end of the monument. Monument identified in 2013 on Lidar imaging (Steve Davis, UCD School of Archaeology). This possible cursus consists of two parallel earthen banks (Wth c. 4.5m; H c. 0.5m) which are 36-39m apart, aligned roughly E-W, and visible over a distance of over 600m (Corlett 2014, 23). At the upper, eastern end the cursus has an open terminal, with the southern bank stopping some distance short of the cairn, though this bank appears to have been robbed out (ibid.). The downslope portion of both banks has been largely levelled but is visible on aerial photographs and Lidar imaging (ibid.). A similar possible cursus monument has been identified on Keadeen Mountain, Co. Wicklow (WI027-089----), with examples in other counties including one on Brewel Hill (KD032-058----) in Co. Kildare and two in Co. Carlow, at Knockendrane (CW020-026----) and Coolasnaghta (CW020-027----).

Situated in the valley of the NW-SE Avonmore River, on the SW bank with the stream c. 50m to the NE. Drainage works uncovered a number of dressed timbers and a subsequent archaeological excavation (14E0365) financed by the National Monuments Service recorded the remains of a watermill. An earthen platform (Wth 6.8m E-W) appearing in a section together with the base of its drystone-built N (Wth 1.5m; max. H 0.8m) and S walls supported the mill building, which would have had a wooden superstructure. Portions of the original head-race appeared in sections of the modern drainage together with timbers on the upstream side, suggesting that it had a timber-lined head-race. A large base-beam (L 5m plus; Wth 0.5-0.7m; T 0.3m plus) with mortises on its upper side 27m from the platform could be the dam of a mill-pond. Some post-medieval pottery, late 17th century clay pipes and hand-made bricks were recovered. Fragments of 18 timbers were recorded and re-buried at the location. They consisted largely of base-plates or oak stakes. The remains are interpreted as those of a vertical undershot-wheeled mill, and one of the timbers produced a dendrochronological date of AD 1679 +- 9 years. (Hayden 2014; 2015)

This stone (c. 1m long) has been dressed to a cylindrical shape and has an undressed knob-like terminal. Although considered as a possible phallic symbol (correctly doubted by Malone 1988, 124)  this is a jostle stone or stop-bollard, one of a pair that would have been used on either side of a gateway to protect both jambs and carriage wheels from damage. The knob-like undressed end would have acted as the anchor in the ground. It probably dates to the 18th/19th century. The stone had formerly leant against the north wall of the church (WA042-019001-) and was missing for a number of years until returned to the site in 2014. The stone is in the care of the Office of Public Works (KK019-137----).

Not marked on any edition of the OS maps, this possible hillfort was discovered from an analysis of LiDAR data by James O'Driscoll of UCC (O'Driscoll 2013). Situated on the S spur of Tuckmill Hill overlooking the town of Baltinglass 900m to the SW.  Rathnagree hillfort (WI027-010----) 600m to N and Rathcoran hillfort (WI027-026001-) 380m to ENE.  Outline of monument barely visible on Digital globe aerial photograph taken November 2011.  Site consists of a sub-circular shaped area (approx. int. diam. 129m NE-SW; 152m NW-SE) enclosed by a low barely visible earthen bank (approx. Wth 4.5m; H 0.2m) which encompasses an area measuring  c. 1.43 ha. There are indications of an internal ditch, visible as a shallow depression inside this bank.  The geophysical survey carried out under consent no. 12R0042 revealed a 10m wide opening on the northern side of the enclosure. It may be an original entrance, but this remains to be confirmed. The E quadrant of the hillfort is crossed by a townland boundary running NE-SW, which comprises of an older wall of smaller stones now covered by boulders from recent field clearance.  There are no features in the level interior of the enclosure, apart from a few large boulders. There are no obvious internal features visible in either the geophysical results or the LiDAR data. The entire site area was investigated by magnetic gradiometry survey in 2012, as part of a landscape study of the Baltinglass hillforts.  In July 2015 an excavation under licence no. 15E0320 was conducted by Professor William O'Brien of University College Cork. This work was undertaken as part of a research project on prehistoric hillforts in Ireland, based in University College Cork with funding from the Irish Research Council. The investigation at Sruhaun involved a single excavation trench which was excavated across the enclosing element on the S side of the hillfort. This 8m by 2m trench was aligned NNE-SSW and cut across the line of the enclosing bank on the S side of the hillfort to the W of the townland boundary. Excavation confirmed the presence of two ditches directly inside the remains of a low bank of stones. There are indications of intense burning at the base of this bank, with samples of charcoal recovered for radiocarbon dating (results pending). There are no artifact finds from the excavation (O'Brien 2015, 1).

The Ordnance Survey Letters of 1838 mention a burial ground where it is referred to as 'Carricknagross grave yard' (O'Flanagan 1927, 105).  Stone cross located in SW quadrant of this burial ground (WI016-014----).  'Cornagrus graveyard' recorded in 1943 by Liam Price who described the monument as following; 'A bank of large stones or boulders and earth surrounds a space about 32yds in diameter.  Inside all that is to be seen is a number of boulders and stones, many of them covered by moss, but in one place there is a cut-stone cross (approx. dims. H 12 ins. [0.3m]; Wth 6 ins. [0.15m]).  It is in two pieces; I don't know if they were originally joined and have been broken, or not, but by putting the cross-head on the pillar it makes quite a good cross.  The pillar is standing in the earth; it can be shaken, so is not deep, but I did not dig to the bottom of it.  There is no sign of carving on it.  It is in the SW part of the enclosure.  It is at the end of some stones which have roughly the shape of a grave, but this might be accidental.  Burke said that people say a priest was buried there' (Corlett and Weaver 2002, 507-08).  The dry-stone wall forms a cashel-like enclosure (WI016-014----) which along with the stone cross located inside may suggest a possible ecclesiastical enclosure.

Aalen (1963, 189) describes booley huts in the townland of Knocknadroose as particularly good examples comprising loose granite boulders in a variety of shapes and sizes (usually rectangular but sometimes round and oval).  They appear to have been located in the area of forestry plantation to the N of 'Carricknagross graveyard' (WI016-014001-).  A booley site recorded by Con Costelloe in this location (pers. comm. Barry Dalby) may be the same site as that recorded by Aalen.  Several hut sites also visible at this location on Digital Globe aerial photograph taken July 2013.  One of these hut sites is visible as a sub-rectangular shaped structure located 170m NW of Carricknagross graveyard (WI016-014----).
This appears to be the Booley hut described in 1949 by Liam Price (Corlett and Weaver 2002, 507) as following: 'the remains of a building.  It was about 14yds long and about 7yds wide, narrowing at one end - roughly rectangular.  Drystone walls, the original part about 2 or 3ft high, with mores stones built up on top to 5 or 6ft.  There had been a cross-wall, but it was gone: it made a room at the wider end, 8 or 10ft broad.  There was a doorway at the SE corner.  E and SE of the house was a small double enclosure or haggard.  This was called the 'Boolia House'.

Ring-barrow situated on the upper slope of a proposed development site with views of Bray Head to the E, Sugar Loaf Mountain to the SE, and Djouce mountain to the S.  The public road located 70m to N marks the townland boundary with Parknasilloge.   Unclassified megalithic tomb (WI007-021----) 370m to NNE, motte castle (WI007-018001-) 300m to SSW, St. Moling's holy well (WI007-016----) 550m to W.  
A detailed gradiometer survey was conducted by J. M. Leigh Surveys Ltd. under licence No. 18R0026 in the townland of Powerscourt Demesne, which identified a possible triple-ditched barrow (approx. overall diam. 25m).  The site consists of a small circular area (approx. diam. 8m) enclosed by three widely spaced circular ditches.  The outer circular ditch has a diameter of 25m, the middle ditch 16m and the inner ditch 8m (Leigh 2018, 4).  Archaeological test trenching was undertaken by Irish Archaeological Consultancy Ltd. on behalf of Lota View Holdings Limited, under licence No. 18E0045 in order to archaeologically assess the results of the geophysical survey. The test trenching confirmed the presence of a probable barrow (c. 25m diameter), with three enclosing ditches. No evidence of a burial or cremated remains was identified during the test trenching (Lynch and Kavanagh 2018, i).  The south‐western part of the barrow appears to have been removed by agricultural ploughing. Two of the three ditches were identified on the north‐eastern side of the site, although the outer ditch was sealed by a spread of archaeological material. The inner ditch was found to have a depth of 0.34m, which suggests that the entire monument has been subject to some truncation due to ploughing.  A number of lithics were recovered during testing, including a quartz core, several individual pieces of quartz and a piece of flint debitage. The items were all recovered from the archaeological spread (C7) and the fill of one of the barrow ditches (ibid., 7).

Archaeological monitoring undertaken at Monalin, Newtownmountkennedy, Co. Wicklow, during construction works for Phase 5 and Phase 5a of the Tower Homes development by Irish
Archaeological Consultancy Ltd, under licence 19E0194 uncovered the remains of total of 133 features of probable archaeological provenance were identified in the Phase 5 area. The results of this monitoring were summarised by the excavators as following; 'These features comprise a largely diffuse spread of pits, possible hearths, possible post holes and stakeholes, a number of possible kiln features (WI013-122----) and a large enclosure of c. 50m diameter. These features will be impacted on by the development. It is recommended to fully excavate and record the features in order to preserve the site by record.  The Phase 5 area is the footprint of two fields of pasture to the immediate west of the footprint of the development routeway, monitored during phase 4 of the current development works. The south field is bounded on its south side by the private laneway which leads to Monalin House (NIAH Reg No. 16307012).
Examination of mapping shows these two fields as areas of pasture, with no additional divisions on both the first and second edition maps.  A programme of geophysical survey followed by targeted archaeological test trenching was carried out within the development area by Margaret Gowan and Co. Ltd. in 2005 (05E1423). No trenches were excavated within the current proposed topsoil strip area, and no features were identified within the current area by the geophysical survey.
Archaeological monitoring of ground disturbance was undertaken in two phases in January (Phase 5a) and April–May (Phase 5) 2019. The work was undertaken by Liza Kavanagh and Barry Lacey of IAC Ltd in the townland of Monalin, Co. Wicklow.  During the course of archaeological monitoring of the Phase 5 area, a total of 133 features of probable archaeological provenance were identified. These features comprise pits, possible hearths, possible post holes and stakeholes, a number of possible kiln features and a large enclosure of c. 50m diameter which straddles the two stripped fields.  
The enclosure is located on level, raised ground overlooking the valley and watercourse to the northeast. It is slightly oval in plan with a northwest–southeast axis of 50m diameter and a northeast–southwest axis of 45m diameter. A number of pit features (c. 22) were identified within the area enclosed by the ditch, however it is as yet uncertain if these features are contemporary. A causewayed entrance, c. 3m wide was identified in the east-southeast of the ditch circuit.
The archaeology in this area is dominated by a large, singe ditched enclosure sited on a level area of high ground overlooking a watercourse and rolling farmland to the north. The siting, size, ditch morphology, location of the causewayed entrance and the retrieval of a ferrous object from the ditchfill suggest that this enclosure represents the remains of a levelled ringfort of early medieval date' (Kavanagh and Duffy 2019, 1-6).

Twenty cross slabs (WI042-019006-/033-) can be seen scattered about Aghowle graveyard (WI042-019003-), all of which have been reused as upright burial markers, which largely explains the main distribution of the cross slabs in the southern part of the graveyard, coinciding with the main area of 18th and 19th century headstones. It is clear that the majority of the cross slabs were originally intended as recumbent slabs, however, their current use as upright headstones means that most of the slabs are partially concealed, thereby limiting the visible features. The majority are schist slabs, except for Cross slabs 2, 11, 15 and 16 which are of granite (Corlett 2019).  
Described by Corlett (2019) as following; 'Cross slab 16 is located immediately south of Aghowle church (WI042-019001-), towards its western end. This granite stone is square in section (32cm x 32cm) and stands 46cm high. The splayed cross is on the south face and has been carved in low relief. The upper transom is notably elongated (24cm tall), and the arms extend the full width of the stone. The cross shaft (4cm wide), which does not appear to be splayed, extends below the ground surface'.

Univallate contour hillfort situated on the summit of a hill [1254ft. OD) in the townland of Colvinstown Upper overlooking Kilranelagh Church (WI027-034001-) and graveyard (WI027-034002-) containing St. Bridget's holy well (WI027-0340013) 500m to W.  Crosoona Rath (WI027-038----) containing two hut sites (WI027-038001-/003-) and an ogham stone (WI027-038002-) lies  500m to E.  On the W slopes of this hill known locally as Kilranelagh Hill there are three recorded cairns (WI027-035---/036-/037-), the stone circle (WI027-039----) and barrow (WI027-040----) described below in the Atlas of Hillforts of Britain and Ireland lies 650m to the ENE.  Outline of enclosing bank of hillfort clearly visible on OSi aerial photographs dating from 2000 and 2005 which clearly shows the upstanding bank from E-S-SW where it fades away.  
Unrecorded hillfort identified in 2014 and described by O'Driscoll (2014) as following; 'A possible hillfort was discovered by the author on the summit of Kilranlagh (385m OD), in the townland of Colvinstown, a prominent hill 5km to the east of Baltingalss town.  The site occupies a total area of approximately 5.33ha, most of which is now under conifer forestry and thick gorse growth.  There are panoramic view from the summit, with particularly striking scenes of the lowlands to the south and south-west'.  Igneous bedrock prevented the application of geophysical survey, with the survey carried out using GPS mapping and aerial photographs.  The enclosing element comprises a stone bank, approximately 14m wide and up to 0.6m high on the west and south-west sides.  The outer side of this bank is revetted with large stone slabs placed horizontally.  A change in vegetation immediately outside the bank may indicate the presence of an outer ditch, approximately 6m wide.  This section of the enclosing elements extends for approximately 140m in length and continues into forestry to the north, abutting a 3-6m high cliff face which forms the southern portion of the hillfort defences.  The eastern section is under dense vegetation and is not visible on the ground.  A curving field pattern recorded in the 1910 edition of the Ordnance Survey may represent the remains of the enclosing elements in this area.  There are no obvious internal features, although these may be obscured by thick heather and scrub growth in some areas (O'Brien and O'Driscoll 2017, 205).  
In 2017 this hillfort was described in the Atlas of Hillforts of Britain and Ireland as a, 'Possible univallate contour fort in commanding positioned surrounding the domed summit of Kilranlagh Hill at SW edge of Wicklow mountains. This fort is one of nine hillforts comprising the Baltinglass hillfort cluster. There are no recorded entrance features. No evidence for any internal features on the surface. Three cairns [WI027-035---/036-/037-], a stone circle and barrow are located on the hilltop, outside the possible hillfort. The ramparts have been heavily affected by commercial forestry plantation. GPS survey (O'Driscoll 2014) has identified a curving rubble stone bank on the western side of the hill. This may be the remains of a possible hillfort. This may correspond with a curving section of bank on the eastern side of the hilltop depicted in first edition Ordnance Survey maps, and with features revealed by aerial photography, which indicate the possible presence of a large enclosure on the summit of Kilranlagh. The interior is overgrown with scrub and is under light blanket bog and is in parts, covered by forestry. First identification and GPS survey by O'Driscoll in 2014.  Recent survey has identified a curving rubble stone bank on the western side of the hill, 140m in length and extending into newly planted forestry. The bank is approximately 14m in width and has exterior facing comprising large slabs. A change in vegetation on the immediate outside may indicate an outer ditch feature. This corresponds with a curving section of bank on the eastern side of the hilltop depicted in first edition Ordnance Survey maps. These may be the remains of a hillfort bank that, when projected, would have enclosed an area 5.33ha.  Enclosure visible at the E, S and W in aerial photography. GPS survey has traced the enclosing elements on the SW and W side of the hilltop. Newly planted forestry prevented the continuation of this survey' (http://hillforts.arch.ox.ac.uk/records/IR0730.html).

Situated at the base of the northwestern slopes of Kilranelagh Hill, on the demesne lands of Kilranelagh House which stands 380m to WSW.  St. Bridget's stone (WI027-031001-) lies immediately to ENE in the adjoining townland of Cloghnagaune.  The enclosing element on the E side of the large enclosure follows the line of the townland boundary with Cloghnagaune.  Remains of a large enclosure recently identified (O’Driscoll 2016, 131-132) which appears to be the same site recorded by Liam Price in his field notes, where he described a large unrecorded enclosure at the base of Kilranelagh Hill, which was subsequently levelled (Corlett & Weaver 2002, 540). Price described the monument as consisting of an outer ditch approximately 10m wide with an internal bank and inner ditch measuring about 6m in width, the bank being ‘only a couple of feet high’ (ibid., 540). O’Driscoll confirmed the presence of this levelled enclosure through his examination of aerial photographs, noting a circular vegetation mark approximately 172m in diameter occupying an area of 2.37ha (2016, 132). The partial cropmark of this enclosure is visible as a curvilinear feature visible from N to E on OSi orthophotos taken 2000.  O’Driscoll stated that the enclosure site and the surroundings were overgrown at that time, making identification of features on the ground difficult. The enclosure site is now almost entirely tree-covered as shown on Digital Globe aerial imagery.

Situated on rising ground in upland area below the summit of Kilranelagh Hill with cairn (WI027-035----) 220m to S and hillfort (WI027-097----) 350m to SSE.  In area of modern forestry overlooking Kilranelagh church (WI027-034001-) and graveyard (WI027-034002-) 210m to W.   On the hillside there are a group of approximately 20 large quartz boulders (H 1.5m) that are white in colour and are known locally as 'The White Stones'.  The boulders cover an area approx. 80m x 30m.  The stones may be a natural or geological feature which became a prominent landmark in the medieval cultural landscape of the region. 
In 1947 Liam Price wrote the following description about the stones on the side of Kilranelagh Hill; 'Drove to the angle of the road between Cloghnagaune and Kilranelagh S of Spinans Bridge, and walked up the old roadway leading to the graveyard. As one drives through Eadestown one sees the white stones on the side of Kilranelagh Hill and coming along the road to Spinans Bridge they are very conspicuous, a group of white stones together on the NW slope of the hill. I do not know any other hill with a group of white stones like this on it.  Just before coming to the graveyard I turned to the left and crossed the fence into Colvinstown Upper, E of the ruined cottages, and went up the hill. The white stones are big blocks of white quartz: there is a scattered outcrop of white quartz here (about 100ft above the 1000ft contour) and some loose blocks, all fairly close together. Above this on the skyline I saw what looked like a cairn [WI027-035----], and on getting to it I found it was a ruined cairn of stones' (Corlett and Weaver 2002, 461).  These stones may be the same feature described in 1930 as following; 'He also pointed out some white stones on the N slopes of Kilranelagh Hill and said they were called "the Griddle Stones", and there were kings buried there' (ibid. 85).  This latter reference may relate to the stone circle (WI027-039----) at Boleycarrigeen.
Michael Russell has suggested that these stones were possibly the same stones known in medieval Ireland as the 'Cows of Aife'.  The saga of the historical cycle in early Middle Irish, known as Fingal Rónáin recounts the tale about how Rónán mac Aeda, King of Leinster killed his only son, Máel-Fhothartaig.  The saga contains the following passage which refers to these stones; ‘Go then tomorrow,’ said Congal, ‘and hunt at the Cows of Aife.'’ (The ‘Cows of Aife’ are stones which are on the side of the mountain.) They are like white cows from afar. ‘Go and hunt there. And the woman shall send her mistress to a tryst with us, and I will put her from you.’ ‘It shall be done,’ said her mistress to her' (Meyer 1892, 378-80).

Unrecorded wedge tomb identified by Christopher J. Darby in 2010 which was followed up by a rescue excavation carried out by Chris Corlett under licence no. 10E0131.  The results of this excavation were summarised as following; 'The site, at Carrigacurra, Ballyknockan, is situated on the edge of the shoreline of the Poulaphuca Reservoir and was first identified by Christopher J. Darby in March 2010. The site is located on the edge of the normal reservoir levels, and would therefore only be inundated when the water levels are at their highest. However, this is the area that is most prone to long-term and consistent erosion by the reservoir. The sand that has partially sealed the site and thereby preserved it over the last number of years is now itself being actively eroded by the reservoir, and the high water levels recorded in 2009 may have significantly contributed to the removal of sand and the resulting exposure of the site (which may explain why it has gone unnoticed until now). This recent erosion had compromised the stability of the site and made it more prone to erosion by the reservoir on the western and southern sides.
Prior to excavation the site appeared to consist of a burial chamber (0.45m wide and 1m long, open at the south-west) placed off-centre within a U-shaped kerb setting (2.1m north-west/south-east x 2.5m) retaining cairn material. Excavation suggests that there were two main phases of use. The initial phase consisted of the construction of the chamber, surrounding cairn and retaining kerb. The chamber was built off-centre within the cairn and retaining kerb and measured 1.2m long and 0.45m wide. The chamber was formed by two large slabs on the southern side, three on the opposite side, and two end stones. The kerb was best preserved at the south and rear. While there was a large amount of stone on the northern side, only one was clearly set. Several others may originally have formed part of the kerb but may have become dislodged by the reservoir at this side. The kerbstones and cairn material lay on a light-brown clay which appears to represent the old sod. This was not present within the burial chamber, where instead a grey silt was present at the lowest levels. The structure can be best compared with wedge tombs of the early Bronze Age (another wedge tomb in the general area is situated at Sroughan, c. 5.5km to the north). No dating evidence was forthcoming for the construction of the tomb, but evidence for this may be preserved beneath the cairn material and surrounding kerb, which was not excavated. There was no evidence for a primary burial within the tomb, but this may be due to later disturbance of the tomb during the early Iron Age.
Whatever about the date of the initial construction of the tomb, it is clear that it was reconfigured and probably reused during the early Iron Age. This phase was represented by a layer of charcoal that was placed within the main chamber and beyond the tomb. This dense charcoal layer (50mm thick) was identified by Ellen O’Carroll as consisting of hazel and oak. Hazel samples from this layer were sent for 14C dating and returned a date of 760–414 bc. There was no evidence for primary burials sealed beneath this charcoal layer, so perhaps the interior was cleaned out prior to the placement of this material within the chamber. There was no evidence for in situ burning of the clay beneath the charcoal layer, clearly indicating that it was deliberately placed here. The charcoal layer did not appear to be randomly dumped, but instead was apparently carefully placed within the chamber. The charcoal also extended north and east of the tomb, but notably was not present beneath the kerbstones of cairn material. The charcoal layer also occurred throughout a void between the chamber and the large kerbstone at the north. It is not clear if this void represents an original chamber or if it was created during this reuse of the site.
Within the rear of the main chamber three stones were found sitting on the charcoal, and the evidence indicated that the chamber was deliberately reduced in size after the charcoal had been placed within. This certainly implies that the intention was to reuse the main chamber for the purpose of burial – perhaps this was also the purpose of what appears to be the new chamber adjacent to it. However, if this was the case, any trace of burial was removed by the reservoir' (www.excavations.ie. No. 836; Corlett 2013, 266-7).

Detailed gradiometer survey in this area identified two clear circular ditch-type responses, correlating with the location of several curving crop marks, measuring c. 11.25m and 12.25m in diameter and several other responses of potential interest. Following on from the geophysical survey, a programme of testing was undertaken in 2017 by Rob Lynch and Enda Lydon of IAC under licence no. 17E0292 (Lynch and Lydon 2017).  Three areas of archaeology were identified in the testing assessment (Archaeological Areas 1–3). The remains are likely to be Bronze Age in date and are similar to other sites that have been recorded within the surrounding landscape. The core of Archaeological Area 1 comprises the two circular anomalies, an outer enclosure and associated features as identified in the geophysical survey and aerial photography in the southwestern portion of the site.
Monument consisted of 'a large penannular enclosure truncated at W by a ring-ditch (WI013-128----) that was in turn truncated by a later kiln (WI013-132---) and large pit to the E and by a modern sand extraction quarry to the NW. The sand and gravel quarry destroyed the NW quadrant of the ditch. The enclosure was accessed through a causewayed entrance (Wth 2m) at S.  Quite degraded  fragments of animal bone were recovered throughout the ditch fills while a small amount of burnt bone was also recovered. The artefacts retrieved from the ditch fills suggest a possible later prehistoric date for the enclosure.  Four pits with in-situ funerary vessels were recorded within the penannular enclosure, external of the two ring-ditches. Pit C311 was located c. 2.5m to the northeast of ring-ditch C343 and it contained an inverted encrusted urn' (Ní Cheallacháin and Spencer 2020, 13-15).

Monument consisted of a 'heavily disturbed burial ground measuring c. 12.4m x 6m and containing twelve burials and seven clusters of disarticulated human bone was identified in the northeast of the site within a localised area of sand within a geological ridge of gravel.
This gravel ridge appears to have been chosen specifically for the location of the burials as no
burials were identified outside of the gravel deposit. All the burials were oriented roughly
SW-NE apart from Sk12. Although historic truncation though ploughing action had disturbed
most of the grave cuts, they all appeared to be rounded rectangular in shape and very
shallow. The grave of Sk9 was the most undisturbed grave with a depth of 0.2m
recorded and a linear placement of large cobbles along the grave cut interpreted as a
possible stone lining. The grave of Sk11 may also have had a stone lining as
five medium-sized stones appeared to line the cut at the northeast end. The majority
of grave fills consisted of moderately compact silty sand with common small stone and gravel
inclusions, while the graves of Sk 6 and Sk 7 were filled with a looser sandy
silt. The graves of Sk 10 and Sk 12 were filled with silty gravels. No grave cut could be determined for the sub-circular deposit of grave fill C227 surrounding Sk 4, which was similar in consistency to the other fills, or for C229 surrounding Sk 5 which comprised of more compact silty sand. All the graves contained fragmented human remains with graves C252, C255 and C257 containing more complete human skeletons. The graves were located across the sandy
deposit C214 in loosely defined rows, with graves C255 and C257 (containing skeletons 10
and 11) abutting each other. Half of the burials contained no artefacts, but flint
was recovered from the fills of four graves, while a metal loop was recovered from the
gravefill of Sk 8. Significantly, a fragment of highly degraded antler tine was retrieved
from the gravefill of Sk 6. The location of the antler near the skull suggests that it may
have been deliberately placed. All of the graves were covered by plough soil C263 which
extended across Area 2 and consisted of moderately loose gravelly silt with frequent stone
inclusions and also contained disarticulated bone B15' (Ní Cheallacháin and Spencer 2020, 30).

Archaeological excavation was undertaken by Yvonne Whitty at Rathcoran House (St Joseph's Convent), Baltinglass, County Wicklow within the constraint area for Baltinglass Historic Town (WI027-024----) in December 2018 under licence No. 18E0686.  The excavation results were described by Whitty (2021, 15-16) as follows; 'Two archaeological sites were identified; Area 1 and Area 2 within the greenfield area to the west of Rathcoran House. This is an area where a roadway and carparking will be located. Intensive test trenching was completed in this area to confirm the extent of the archaeology identified. The entire footprint of the roadway and parking area was stripped between both sites.  All features were subsequently fully excavated by hand.
Area 1 is located adjacent to Rathcoran House in Test Trench 1.  A group of two postholes which appear to be joined by a slot and a cremation burial pit have been grouped together based on their proximity and the fact that all these features were sealed by large sub angular flat stones.  The most northerly feature was a cremation pit C6 which measured 0.76m x 0.60m and was 0.18m in depth. The pit appeared to have been left open for some time after its excavation as the basal fill C15 was the result of natural siltation. The middle fill C14 was pyre material mixed with cremated bone. Osteological analysis indicates that the remains of an adult and possible juvenile were deposited in this pit.  Analysis of a sample of charcoal recovered from the fill C14 identified alder and oak charcoal in pit fill C14 which was used as fuel for the pyre. This sample has been radiocarbon dated to the Late Bronze Age (UBA-43608, 2847+-34, 1118-916BC at two sigma calibration)'.

Archaeological excavation was undertaken by Yvonne Whitty at Rathcoran House (St Joseph's Convent), Baltinglass, County Wicklow within the constraint area for Baltinglass Historic Town (WI027-024----) in December 2018 under licence No. 18E0686.  The excavation results were described by Whitty (2021, 22-3) as follows; 'Archaeological Area 2 comprised a large shallow pit was located at the southeast extent of the development in Trenches 1 and 8.  This isolated feature C23, comprises a large sub rectangular pit which was northeast to southwest aligned measuring 3.9m in length, 2.2m in width and was 0.40m in depth (Figure 18- Figure 20, Plate 11 and Plate 12). It contained five fills C24-C28. The primary fill C24 a black sandy silt contained slag which consisted exclusively of partial and complete smithing hearth cakes with weights of single examples ranging from 262g to 1386g (Rondolez, Appendix 7 Metalworking Report). Also contained within C23 where several fragments of clay tuyeres were recovered (18E0686:231-8). The largest piece (266g) consisted of the lower part of a vitrified tuyere front and showed that the original tuyere was truncated cone-shaped with a flat front which had a ‘slag beard’ attached to it. Other pieces represent heat-affected tuyere wall fragments. The primary fill was overlain with a redeposited natural C25, followed by smithing debris material C26 a layer of redeposited natural C27 sealed this layer and the uppermost natural siltation layer C28 accumulated after the pit was abandoned.'  The metal analysis completed by Rondolez indicates that this assemblage represents the waste of secondary blacksmithing, likely the production of large iron objects or substantial quantities of smaller ones. This activity took place outside of the area of excavation and was dumped into the pit C23. The date of the assemblage is most likely of either early or late medieval in date'.

This final excavation report details the results of an excavation under licence No. 18E0608 at the site of a residential and commercial development at Richview House Bellvue Hill, Delgany, County Wicklow.  The results of this excavation were described by the excavator, Yvonne Whitty as follows; 'Located on elevated ground sloping gently to the east within the grounds of and in adjacent fields to Richview House and associated gatehouse which overlooks the Irish Sea to the east. The site comprised a cremation burial site containing five pit burials in a linear east-west alignment over an area 6m by 2m. This site was identified in the north-east part of the field at ITM 727537 711317. An area 10m by 10m was opened around the features in order to establish the nature and extent of the archaeology and additional test trenching was undertaken to ensure that there were no enclosing features surrounding the burial site. There was no trace of any associated features ring-ditches or of any cairn/mound which covered the burials.  Excavation was completed between the 9th-12th October 2018 under licence 18E0608 by the licence holder with the assistance of an archaeological supervisor.  Given the possibility that two phases of burial were apparent at Delgany two C14 dates were obtained which confirmed this assumption, this was a multi phased burial site spanning the Late Bronze and Iron Age. Differing fuel was chosen for the pyre in the Late Bronze Age (oak) and Iron Age (ash). The cremated remains comprised five adults and a juvenile. This site also adds to our understanding of climate deterioration as evidenced in the pollen record in the Late Bronze Age and Iron Age in the locality of Delgany, as evidenced by charcoal analysis which is discussed further in this report. The site is also significant in that it is only the second confirmed Iron Age cremation pit in Wicklow. It also brings the total to sixty-nine Iron Age cremation burial sites so far recorded in Ireland.
The features were exposed 0.35m below the topsoil and comprise a linear cluster of five cremation burials in shallow pits that were contained within an area measuring 6m east west by 2m north-south. A total of five cremation burials aligned east to west were excavated and the fills were retained in their entirety for post excavation analysis. The pits were aligned over a distance of 6m. Four pits were clustered together at the west and a single outlying pit was located at 1.85m to the east of the other four burials. Post excavation analysis has confirmed that there were two phases of burial at Delgany. The burials were situated in a linear east to west alignment. There was no trace of a mound, carin or ring ditch surrounding the burials. Radiocarbon dating has demonstrated that the site was in use during the Late Bronze Age and Iron Age. Burial 5 (C12) has been dated to the Late Bronze Age (UBA-43516, 2829+-25, 1052-906 BC at two sigma calibration) and Burial 1 (S1, C4) has been radiocarbon dated to the Iron Age (UBA-43613, 1747+-25, 242-382 AD at two sigma calibration).
Burial 5 was the most westerly and Burial 1 the most easterly and an outlier from the group. Charcoal analysis from the five cremation burials provides a clue to the phasing of the site. Context related variation is clearly evident in the burials with Burial 1 (C4) and Burial 2 (C6) dominated by ash (O Donnell, 2020). Burial 1 dates to the Iron Age and Burial 2 is located west of Burial 1. In contrast, Burials 3, 4 and 5 (C8, C10, and C12) are all dominated by oak. It is the authors assumption based on the fuel source and the location of the cremation pits that Burials 3,4 and 5 date to the Late Bronze Age and Burials 1 and 2 date to the Iron Age' (Whitty 2021).

Archaeological test trenching by Yvonne Whitty under Licence 20E0571 for an 8.4-hectare extension to the existing quarry revealed two features of archaeological significance were identified at the southeast corner of the proposed quarry 3m from the field boundary and access laneway which will be preserved in situ. Following consultation with the client this area will not be excavated; the boundary ditch along the entire length of the proposed quarry will not be removed and a buffer of 10m will be left from the boundary ditch to the limit of excavation to store topsoil and prevent undermining of the laneway. There will be no topsoil stored at the location of the pits which will be fenced off with post and sheep wire to prevent accidental damage from wheel ruts.  
The results of the testing were described by Whitty (2021) as follows; 'Temporary fencing covering an area of 25 square meters has been erected around the features in the interim and the limit of excavation will be 7m from these features which was devoid of archaeology. The field is currently under pasture and it may take several years for the quarry to reach this limit. Two features of archaeological significance were identified at the east corner of the proposed quarry extension 3m from the field boundary and access laneway which will be preserved in situ.  The two shallow pits filled with fractured, heat-affected subangular sandstone stones and black, ashy soil were exposed). The fill of both pits was identical and similar to the typical fills of burnt mounds. The pits were 0.75m apart. The most easterly pit had a diameter of 1.15m - 1.17m and a small slot showed a depth of 0.28m at the deepest, central point. The most westerly pit had a diameter of 0.90 - 1.09m. An area 15m by 10m was opened around the pits which was constrained by a lane to the north. No other features were encountered and no artefacts were recovered. If related features are present'.

Archaeological test trenching was carried out by Muireann Ní Cheallacháin of IAC Archaeology under licence 21E0133 which followed on from a geophysical survey conducted in December 2020 by John Nicholls of Target Geophysics under licence 20R0236.  The results of this test trenching were summarised as follows; 'A total of 148 trenches were excavated across the site measuring 6820 linear metres.  Testing at AA1 confirmed the presence of a heavily truncated rectangular ditched enclosure (possible original int. diameter: 75m x 65m) and the partial remains of an annex to the south of the enclosure as identified in the geophysical survey.  At least 30m (c.50%) of the western arm of the enclosure ditch along with an area measuring c.75m x 30m (c. 40%) of the enclosure’s interior have been heavily truncated by the construction of the distribution road. Testing has also revealed that the entire eastern extent of the rectangular enclosure ditch has been heavily truncated by construction activity associated with the distribution road. While the enclosure ditch ranges in width from 2.3m to 4m, the relatively shallow nature of the surviving enclosure ditch (0.7m-1m) and some of the habitation features suggests the site has been truncated by agricultural activity over time. A large pit of dumped post-medieval rubble material possibly associated with the demolition of Downshire house and two gravel extraction pits were also identified within AA 1a suggesting further modern truncation of the site as a whole.
Items recovered from the investigation of the enclosure ditches and internal features include fragments of lignite/jet bracelet, flint lithics, stone tools, metalworking waste of iron and possible non-ferrous metals, kiln or furnace furniture and a possible crucible fragment.  The form of the enclosure and annex and the habitation and metalworking evidence along with the recovery of a lignite/jet bracelet suggests that it may be the highly fragmented remains of an early medieval ringfort' (Ní Cheallacháin 2021, 17-19).

Situated on the grounds of the former Rectory to the immediate N, 310m to the NE of Blessington church and graveyard.  Holy Well (WI005-026----) known as 'Toberanbrick' 200m to SE.  Archaeological monitoring was carried out on 27th October 2020 by Grace Fegan of Shanarc Archaeology Ltd., prior to development works within the grounds of The Rectory (former), Kilbride Road, Blessington.  The results of the excavation were described by Grace Fegan (2021) as follows; 'The development works comprised the stripping of topsoil in advance of the construction of housing under planning reference 20/108.  Human remains in the form of one supine extended burial and one poorly preserved and truncated burial were identified during monitoring on Wednesday 28th October 2020. Osteoarchaeologist Dr Linda Lynch visited the site on Friday 30th October.  The excavation area was defined and underwent full archaeological excavation under licence No. 20E0301 between 17th November and 8th December 2020.  The site appears to be the remains of a medieval burial ground, which was greatly disturbed by later agricultural and domestic activity and also by industrial activity, associated perhaps with the construction of the Rectory in the late 19th century.
The burial ground is not apparent in any available cartographic or documentary sources. However, there is a 13th century written reference to a parish church called Capella de Villa Cumyn, the location of which is uncertain. This church is believed to be located at the site of Scurlock’s Graveyard [WI005-027----] in the townland of Crosscoolharbour, to the north, but there is a possibility that the church was located much closer to the village of Blessington (C. Corlett, pers comm). Further documentary research will be required in order to explore the possible connection between the church site and the remains uncovered during this excavation.
The preliminary results suggest an initial phase of formal E-W oriented burials and a later phase of more informal, mostly infant burials. However, further osteoarchaeological, dating and artefact analysis will be required in order to fully establish the phasing of activity on site' (Fegan 2021, 32).

Three lintel-burials of possible 6th-7th century date were uncovered during construction works by Wicklow County Council on Thursday 25th March 2021. It was not possible to preserve the burials in situ, so preservation by record was the appropriate archaeological mitigation strategy in this area under Licence No 21E0208 by Yvonne Whitty of De Faoite Archaeology.  The results of this excavation were summarised by Yvonne Whitty as follows; 'Excavation was completed between the 31st March and the 7th April 2021 under licence 21E0208 by the licence holder with the assistance of an archaeological supervisor Ivor Kenny.  The development site is irregular in plan and is divided into two green areas by a road which leads into two housing developments Mountainview and Sycamore Drive. The south of the development site is bound by Rockview Close and to the west is an un-named road which leads into the village of Newtownmountkennedy. A large rock outcrop is located to the northwest of the burial area.  The development is for Part VIII Approval for 22 Social Housing Units at Mountainview, Moneycarroll, Newtownmountkennedy, County Wicklow and all associated site works. The burials were located at the northeast end of the site at Unit 16, the foundation of this building would have impacted upon the burials. 
The site comprised three isolated lintel graves and preliminary analysis indicates that these were all females over the age of 35. However post excavation analysis is still ongoing and all results will be contained within a final report. They were located below what appears to be a redeposited natural C20 which was 0.42m in average thickness. There was no evidence of a mound in the north of west section face, however the area has been subject to significant disturbance as the Dublin Corporation watermain runs in the road adjacent the site.
Burial 1 was the most southerly and was WNW to ESE aligned and the most poorly preserved of the three burials. The cut C3 was sub-rectilinear in plan and was a lintel grave with upright trimmed blue/grey slate stones lining the sides C12 and top of the grave-cut C9. Occasional round packing stones C12 were visible around the cut of the grave at the head of the grave and behind the side lintel stones on the north and south side of the grave cut. The foot of the grave was clearly defined with a slate stone and it was not clear if the top of the grave where the skull was also defined in a similar manner, however these may have been removed during site clearance works.  The top of the grave was lined with five large lintel stone slabs, C9 which had collapsed in on top of the adult burial and it was unclear if this burial was shroud wrapped given the degree of preservation, however further osteological analysis is required. Preliminary analysis indicates that this burial was that of an adult female. It is also tentatively suggested that this burial had a stone placed on the upper left chest area, however this could also be a collapsed lintel stone.  
Burial 2 was positioned in between Burials 1 and 3 and was WNW to ESE aligned and similar in alignment to Burial 1. The cut C5 was sub-rectilinear in plan and was a lintel grave with trimmed blue/grey upright slate stones lining the sides C13 and also the top of the grave C10. The side stones at the southern side of the grave C13 had collapsed in revealing sub rounded packing stones C17 which lined the edge of the cut prior to the placement of the slate side stones. Both the foot and top of the grave were clearly defined with lintel stones, packing stone was also visible at the head of the grave. There was very little grave fill C6 surrounding Burial 2 indicating that the grave construction with the lintel stones formed a cavity which also aided in preservation of the burial which preliminary analysis suggests is that of a female. The hands were placed over the pelvis and the foot bones were located close together indicating that this burial was probably wrapped in a shroud prior to burial.
Burial 3 was the furthest north of the three burials and was of a different alignment that the other burials which were WNW-ESE, Burial 3 was E-W aligned. It was also the best preserved of all three burials. The cut C7 was sub-rectilinear in plan and was a lintel grave with trimmed blue/grey slate stones C14 lining the sides of the grave-cut and also the top of the grave C11. The side stones C14 at the northern side of the grave had collapsed in revealing sub rounded packing stones C18 which lined the edge of the cut prior to the placement of the slate side stones. Both the foot and top of the grave were clearly defined with side stones C14. Packing stone C18 was also visible at the head of the grave. There was very little grave fill C8 surrounding Burial 3 indicating that the grave construction with the lintel stones formed a cavity which also aided in preservation of the burial as there was very little soil in the grave. Preliminary analysis suggests burial 3 is a female. The hands were placed over the pelvis and the feet were tightly placed together indicating that this burial was wrapped in a shroud prior to burial. The right leg of this burial was crossed over the left leg. Also the burial was laid diagonally within the grave cut perhaps to accommodate the body within the cut which may have been too small for the body' (Whitty 2021, 22-7).

Situated on a low N-S running ridge c. 320m WSW of the tip of Wicklow Head and c. 3.3kms to the ESE of the centre of Wicklow Town (OD c. 73m). Located on a local high point in a locally undulating landscape with a N-S running gully located adjacent (c. 90m) to the E between this site and the coastline (where there are steep rocky sea cliffs), and between the original Wicklow Head Lighthouse (NIAH Reg. No. 16403102; this site) and the later Wicklow Head Lighthouse (NIAH Reg. No. 16403101) located 130m to the E. The immediate area consists of (an enclosed) rough unimproved scrubland in all directions from this site with pastureland, defined by linear field boundaries, located to the W, SW, and NW of this site after c. 250ms. The adjacent signal station\towers in the signal station chain were located at Mizen Head (SMR WI036-022----), located c. 12.25kms to the SSW, now demolished, and at Ballygannon (WI013-145----), located c. 17.28kms to the NNW, now demolished (site unknown). The site of this signal station at Wicklow Head is located c. 915m SE of a (penal) church site (WI025-017001-) located at Bride’s Head, and c. 790ms N\NNE of a coastal promontory fort (WI031-110----) located on a small narrow peninsula to the SW of Dunbar Head. 

The signal station was apparently established at the original (upper) Wicklow Head Lighthouse (NIAH Reg. No. 16403102) which was constructed in 1778-9 (one of two lights built at Wicklow Head between c. 1769-79). The six-stage lighthouse is 30m tall and has a distinctive octagonal-plan. It was designed by John Trail whilst serving as architect\engineer to the Commissioners of Revenue (Rynne 2006, 406). These two lighthouses were later superseded by two new lighthouses (NIAH Reg. No. 16403101) to the E, built 1816-8. It is not entirely clear if the signal crew of the signal station were accommodated at the upper or lower lighthouse but it seems more likely (for visibility and signalling purposes) that the signal station was at the upper lighthouse on the high ground to site. It is thought that the signal mast was the only addition made to the site when the signal station was established, and that the signal crew were housed within existing buildings to site (Kerrigan 1995, 161). The signal mast was erected by September 1805 (Kerrigan 1995, 276). 

The signal station was part of a system of over 80 signal stations constructed by the British Board of Ordnance in the first decade of the nineteenth century to warn of the approach of a French invasion fleet. Signalling between sites was accomplished using a naval signal post. The system formed a continuous chain from Malin Head in Donegal to Dublin Bay. It was abandoned by the mid-1810s when the treat of a French invasion diminished (Kerrigan 1995, 157-66).

Situated on level terrain (exact site unknown) on a low-lying site adjacent to E of the coastline, and c. 3.6kms to the ESE of the town of Delgany and c. 3.5kms SSE of Greystones (OD c. 22m). Land rises very gradually inland to the W with obstructed views in all directions. The surrounding landscape is characterised by arable and pastureland defined generally by linear field boundaries, and by a long sandy shoreline with an area of sandy hinterland located adjacent to the E (now occupied by railway line). The adjacent stations in the signal station\tower chain were located at Wicklow Head (WI031-112001-), located c. 17.3kms to the SSE, where the signal crew are thought to have been accommodated at an existing lighthouse, and at Dalkey Hill, Dublin (DU023-072----), located c. 17.1kms to the NNW, where the signal tower survives in an altered format. The possible\approximate site of this signal station at Ballygannon is located c. 1.9kms to the NE of a church site (WI013-029001-) with an associated graveyard (WI013-029002-), located close to the centre of the village of Kilcoole, and c. 3.5kms ESE of another church site (WI013-004001-) with an associated graveyard (WI013-004002-) located to the S end of the village of Delgany.   

The signal station\tower at Ballygannon Signal Station has been demolished, and its exact position and its original form is not known. It is not depicted on the Ordnance Survey first ed. six-inch map, surveyed 1838, which suggests it was removed at an early date. Kerrigan established that construction of a signal tower here began in 1805, and that it was still under construction in 1806. It is not clear if the signal tower was ever completed (Kerrigan 1995, 276). Kerrigan established that the signal mast had been erected by April 1806 (Kerrigan ibid). 

It is notable that this signal station\tower was demolished by the time of the Ordnance Survey first ed. six-inch map series. This also occurred at a number of signal station sites in County Waterford and at least one site in County Wexford, which is in contrast to the situation with the contemporary signal station sites along the NW, W and SW coastlines. There were concerns expressed (in writing) in 1811 by a Mr. Pope, Waterford Agent of the London Assurance Company, that the disused signal station\towers along the Waterford coastline were causing confusion for seafarers who were mistaking these for lighthouses (particularly Hook Head, Wexford) in poor weather, which led to a number of shipwrecks along the Waterford coastline (around Tramore in particular) in c. 1810. These concerns were apparently acted upon with the demolition of a signal station somewhere close to Tramore (probably at Brownstown Head; WA026-098----) by the end of 1811. Perhaps something similar happened with signal station at Ballygannon, Wicklow.  

The signal tower was part of a system of over 80 signal stations constructed by the British Board of Ordnance in the first decade of the nineteenth century to warn of the approach of a French invasion fleet. Signalling between sites was accomplished using a naval signal post. The system formed a continuous chain from Malin Head in Donegal to Dublin Bay. It was abandoned by the mid-1810s when the treat of a French invasion diminished (Kerrigan 1995, 157-66).

On a gentle NE-facing slope. The settlement occurs within a triangular area (80m N-S; 80m E-W) with the apex at the N. The area is defined on the W side by an earth and stone unfaced bank (Wth 2m; H 1m). This bank is a field boundary which continues beyond the settlement. There is a rectangular/trapezoidal building (c. L 22m; Wth 7m) in the N corner of the settlement (known locally as 'The Chapel') defined by an earth and stone bank (Wth 1.5m; H 1m). To the SE there are two ill-defined structures the first of which is the NW end of a small square or rectangular structure. The second larger structure or enclosure (11m x 11m) is also defined by an earth and stone bank and is attached to a field boundary. To the south of these structures are two well preserved houses. The first house (15m x 8m), aligned N-S, is sub-rectangular in plan and is enclosed by a stone wall (Wth 2.2m; H 0.6m). To the E, the second house (c. 9m x 6m), aligned NW-SE, is enclosed by stone walls of similar dimensions to the previous example. To the S of these houses there is another possible house (c. 7m x 6m) and part of a small enclosure. On the E side of the settlement is a C-shaped structure (5m x 4m); there is a narrow depression running into the structure from the W side. This may be a small kiln. Outside the NW side of the triangular area is a small square structure (4m x 4m). An additional feature on the E edge of the settlement may be part of a house or enclosure. The E side of the settlement is defined mainly by a stone wall. Cultivation ridges occur in the fields to the E and W of the settlement.

The town of Bray is situated on the Dargle River and is divided into Little Bray to the N and Great Bray to the S. The manor of Bray was granted to Walter de Ridelesford before 1176 and was resigned to the Crown in 1280. The first reference to a burgage is c. 1225 when de Ridelesford granted a burgage 'opposite my castle beyond the river' to St Mary's Abbey, Dublin. A mill stood below the castle (WI004-001003-) and a number of Roman burials were discovered near the seafront (WI004-004----). (Scott 1913; Davies 1986, 22; Bradley and King 1989, 12-17).

National Monument in state ownership No. 491.  Situated on an E-facing slope overlooking the River Liffey. Rectangular three-storey tower house with a projecting stair turret at the NE angle. It originally had a structure attached at the W side, where the springing of a barrel vault is visible. A doorway above the present entrance gave access from the original building to the later addition. Another barrel vault roofs the third floor in the surviving portion. Ascent to the first floor appears to have been by stairs in the W structure. This floor level has a large fireplace, decorative mouldings on the windows, and a garderobe with a chute built into the wall thickness of the stair turret. The site of another castle (WI005-032----) is indicated on the OS 6-inch map 300m to the E.

properties.notes:
Situated on a small spit of land now extending into the Blessington Reservoir originally overlooking the confluence of the Liffey and King's River. The church and graveyard represent part of the deserted medieval borough of Burgage More and formed part of the lands of the bishops of Glendalough in the twelfth century (MacNeill 1950, 5-6). The remains consist of the foundations of a rectangular walled structure (dims. c. 11m E-W; c. 9m N-S; T 0.8m; H 0.28m)) within a graveyard (dims. c. 55m E-W x c. 70m N-S) defined by a modern wall and by two old roads to the E and W of the site. The graveyard has been damaged by the waters of the reservoir and there are no visible grave-markers. One high cross and portion of another were originally located here but have been removed to the modern, graveyard c. 800m to the N (WI005-04700--). Reynolds (1973, 67) mentions a font at this site but it is now missing and a holy well (WI005-070003-) was also situated here. Burgage More tower house (WI005-070004-) lies close by to the S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Part of a complex of prehistoric sites (WI005-084----, WI005-081----, WI005-083----, WI005-110----, WI005-111----) on the lower western slopes of Lugnagun overlooking Blessington Reservoir. The rectangular gallery (dims. 6m x 1m) is represented by sidestones, flanked on either side by an outer wall or stone setting. There is a single fa¸ade stone at the SE and the kerb is substantially intact, particularly on the N side. The gallery is divided into a slightly wedge-shaped portico (dims. 1.8m x 1.5-1.8m) at the SW end separated from the remainder by two large jambstones with a line of smaller stones between them apparently forming a sill-like feature. A number of prostrate slabs outside the W end of the gallery may be displaced roof-slabs. The cairn (dims. 10.5m x 8.8m) is oval. The tomb is aligned WSW-ENE with the entrance facing SW down a marked slope with a gentler gradient above the site. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 140)

The graveyard of the Church of Ireland in Blessington contains eight 17th-century headstones. These include granite stones erected to Darby Burke (ob. 1690), Richard Benell (ob. 1686), Ann Hiall (ob. 1687), Thomes Lear (ob. 1688), William Beates (ob. 1685) and William Bluomey (ob. 1683), a fragment of the stone erected to Richard Provei (ob. 168-), and a bevelled stone executed in sandstone erected to David Murphy (ob. 1699). The headstone of William Bluomey states that he was the first to be buried in the graveyard. The headstones have recently been re-erected against the N wall of the graveyard.
