Situated on a SE-facing slope of Kippure Mountain, in recently planted forestry. Circular enclosure (diam. 13m) defined by a poorly preserved earthen bank. No indication of an entrance, external fosse or internal features. (Information P. Healy)

Monument inspected 05/03/20201 by Séamus Ó Murchú, archaeologist, Forest Service, DAFM and described as follows; 'Situated c. 10m to the south-west of the forest boundary and c. 16m to the south-west of the public road contiguous to the northern boundary of the forest plantation. Here, the public road is separated from the forest plantation by a fosse, an outer bank and an external fosse. The topography slopes gently to the south-west. At the south-eastern side of the Enclosure is a granite outcrop from which the slope falls away sharply to the southeast before levelling off with the surrounding slope. As a result, when approached from the southeast, the monument appears to be sited on a plateau or shallow ridge on the slope.
The upstanding remains of the Enclosure are in a poor state of preservation however, it is still evident within the forest plantation. The monument measures c. 13m in diameter overall defined by a subtle earth and stone bank. The enclosing element is best preserved on the northern and western sides of the monument. Here, an 8m long earth and stone bank arc from NE—N—W—SW. It has a maximum internal height of 0.3m and maximum external height of 0.1m and measures approximately 3m wide throughout. The western—south-western side of the monument is almost indiscernible. A 6m long earthen bank is evident on the southwestern and southern side of the monument which measures c. 2.1m wide and between 0.05—0. 1m high. The southernmost side of the enclosure is indiscernible before a short, 2m long and 1m wide section of bank material reappears on the south-eastern side. The enclosing element is indiscernible on its eastern side. The interior of the monument has an almost imperceptible slope towards the centre and measures 8—9m in diameter. Trees are growing within the enclosure and either on the surviving portions of the bank or the projected line of the enclosing element. There was no evidence for an internal or external fosse however, the extremely denuded nature of the monument and the trees growing within and on top of the enclosing element suggests that it may have been levelled between the time of Patrick Healy's inspection in the late 20th century and the present inspection and most likely at the time of afforestation. A possible entrance feature was evident in the north-western side of the enclosing element defined by a 0.4m high upright stone on the western side and a cluster of granite cobbles on the eastern side. A possible 1.5m long arc of stone also extended into the monument from the northern bank although this may be a product of the levelling works rather than an internal feature'.

National Monument in state ownership No. 262.  Situated on a small level platform overlooking a marked NE-facing slope with steep ground uphill to the SW. A nave and chancel church (L 10.8m; Wth 5.9m) with walls of irregular uncoursed masonry (H 1.5-2.5m; Wth 0.85m). The gables are substantially intact. The door in the N wall, which is slightly W of the centre, splays inwards and parts of the cut granite jambs survive. There are simple round-headed windows in the E and W gables and a single niche occurs in the S wall towards the W end. The church has been substantially conserved. A rectangular area of rubble and mortar (dims. 4m x 2m) immediately E of the church may represent the foundations of another building. The church is known as Raithín a' Chluig, or 'little rath of the bell'.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Situated on the N summit of a steep-sided N-S ridge in a narrow rocky valley S of the Anglo-Norman town of Hollywood (WI009-017----). The motte consists of a steep-sided mound (dims. 60m N-S; 50m E-W; H 5-6m) which incorporates the spine of the ridge and has a flat top (diam. 15m). The surrounding fosse and external bank are well defined at the W and S and can be traced at the E. To the N a flat- bottomed fosse (Wth 5m; D 2.5m) divides the motte from the level bailey; and there is a centrally located causeway (Wth 3m). Large sections of collapsed masonry occur on the side of the motte and at the base of the fosse at the SW. The bailey consists of a largely natural platform (dims. 50m N-S; 45m E-W) defined by a steep scarp and with traces of earthworks along the E side.

Situated on a gentle W-facing slope overlooking marshy terrain. Bivallate circular ringfort (diam. 23m; max. ext. diam. 41.5m) excavated prior to the construction of the Blessington Reservoir. The site was defined by an earthen bank (Wth 1.5m; H 0.6m) and a fosse (Wth 2.4m; D 1m) with an outer bank (Wth 2.7m; H 0.6m) from SSW-NW-NE. The fosse was separated from the inner bank by a berm (Wth 3-6m) and was partly separated from the outer bank by a second berm (max. Wth 3.4m). There were two narrow gaps (Wth 1m) in the inner bank at the NE and WSW with a more substantial example (Wth 1.5m) at the SSE opposite a causeway in the fosse. A second causeway formed by large stones occurred at the NE but may not have been an original feature. At the S, an L-shaped bank ran from the inner bank outwards across the fosse and then continued eastwards as far as the SSE entrance. Little, other than an arc of irregular paving in the N sector of the interior, was revealed during excavation. (Macalister 1943)

Situated at the foot of a gentle E-facing slope. The church is represented by a very low bank (H 0.1-0.2m) which defines a rectangular structure (dims. 9.5m E-W; 5.3m N-S) towards the W end of a rectangular platform (dims. c. 13m E-W; c. 7.8m N-S). This occurs in the centre of a D-shaped graveyard (dims. 34m E-W; 30m N-S) occupying the SW portion of a larger oval enclosure (dims. c. 48m E-W; 34m N-S). The graveyard is defined at S and W by an earth and stone bank (Wth 1.3-2m; int. H 0.8-1m; ext. H 1.1-1.3m) with a near-vertical external drystone facing. At the E (straight side) the bank abuts a farmtrack which divides the site N-S. The perimeter of the outer enclosure is represented by a slight scarp to the E of the track. An outer fosse (Wth 3m; D 0.3m) occurs at the SW but the bank continues for some distance to the N where it underlies a farmyard wall. A hexagonal block of granite (L 0.73m; Wth 0.66m; T 0.3m) with a subrectangular basin (D 0.04-0.11m) and no drainage hole lies beside the church site and may be a font or a cross-base.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

National Monument in state ownership No. 135.  Situated on a gentle E-facing slope overlooking the Glen of the Downs. A nave and chancel church (dims. 12.85m E-W; 6.55m N-S) of uncoursed rubble with a bellcote at the W end. The door at the W has dressed and chamfered granite jambs, but the arch does not survive. A simple flat-arched window occurs in the gable above the door. There are string courses in the W gable at the level of the top of the walls and the top of the window. The E window has a shallow arch and there are opposing flat-arched windows in the N and S walls at the E end of the church. A small wall niche occurs on each wall at the S end. A modern internal buttress stands against the S wall; the building was restored in 1906. A small granite stoup or font with a circular basin lies in the W end of the church.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Situated on a gentle E-facing slope. The remains of an early 17th-century house probably built for Henry Walsh. The main block (L 14.3m; Wth 7.6m) is gabled and had two storeys with attic. The entrance is at the E with a stair turret directly opposite projecting from the W wall. The wrought jambstones of the door were removed in 1943-4; a shallow armorial recess occurs overhead. Attached at the NE side is a kitchen block (int. dims. 6.9m x 4.9m) of similar construction and height. Substantial chimney stacks survive intact on the N and W walls of the main block. There is no cut stone visible. (Leask, OPW files 1944; Price 1957, 322)

A series of test trenches opened in 2006 (Excavation Licence 06E0113) to the WNW in advance of the construction of a dwelling did not reveal anything of archaeological significance.

Situated on a gentle E-facing slope in Kilcoole village. A nave (int. dims. 8.75m x 5.2m) and chancel (int. dims. 5.6m x 2.93m) church, with an extension to the nave at the W (int. dims. 8.6m x 5.3m), all built of uncoursed rubble. There is a low segmental chancel arch with a tapering opening immediately above. The base of the corbelling for the nave and chancel roofs survives, as does the upper line of the nave roof which projects from the gable above the chancel arch. Simple round-headed windows occur in the E gable and the S wall of the nave with simple tapering windows at a high level in the E and W gables. The S window has bevelled sandstone jambs and arch stones. A modern wall projects 1m from the N and S walls with a gate dividing the nave. The W door is slightly off-centre and has a low segmental arch. The extension at the W is a later addition and has a door, marked only at foundation level, at the W end of the S wall. Both the W and N walls are substantially intact. A granite cross-slab as been placed against the chancel arch at the E end of the nave and a square granite font with rounded corners stands immediately inside the door of the nave. The graveyard is a quadrangular enclosure (dims. 35m E-W; 28m N-S) defined by a 19th-century wall. It contains a large number of early 18th-century headstones. (O'Flanagan 1928, 62-4)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Situated at the W end of an E-W ridge and forming part of the medieval borough of Newcastle (WI019-005----). Earliest references to the castle formerly known as Newcastle McKynegan date to c. 1210-13 (Orpen 1908, 129). Circular level platform (summit dims. 63m E-W; 62m N-S; max. base dims. 102m E-W; 88m N-S) fashioned from a natural ridge and defined by a steep scarp. There are very slight traces of an earthen bank (Wth 3-4m; max. H 0.3m) around the W, N and E edges of the platform. At the E there is a wide fosse (Wth 5m; D 1m) at the foot of the platform scarp which cuts the site off from the rest of the ridge on which it sits. The base of the fosse is 4m below the platform and less than 1m below the external ground level at the E. To the N and S the fosse levels out into a narrow terrace (Wth 5m at the S; 2-5m at the N; Wth of fosse 5-6m at the W). At the W end of the platform are the remains of an Anglo-Norman stone  castle/gatehouse (WI019-005002-) which gives access to the interior of the ringwork in a similar manner to the castle earthwork at Castle Kevin (WI024-003001-).  A causeway (Wth 5m) occurs directly opposite the entrance to the castle and 10m to the W of it. A possibly cobbled approach to the stone castle fans out towards the castle angles from the causeway, edged with a setting of small stones. (CUCAP, BDE 17)  The cropmark of a semi-circular shaped ditch can be seen on aerial photographs which could be the remains of an outer bailey (www.bingmaps.com) (SMR file).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Located against the W wall of Killiskey graveyard (WI019-011001-).  A cylindrical granite block (diam. at top 0.72m-0.74m; H 0.5m) with a circular basin (diam. at top 0.53m; diam. at base 0.43m; D 0.2m). The sides are sloping and the base is dished. A drain hole exists at one side and is recessed into side of basin.  The hole narrows to 2cm across, and expands to 8cm across where it exits the side of the font.
The rim immediately around the mouth of the basin takes the form of a flat ledge (3cm wide) that is slightly lower than the outer circumference of the rim.  This was clearly designed to accommodate a lid. On the outer circumference of the rim are three small holes (one directly above the drain hole).  These are sub-rectangular in shape with rounded bases (ranging from 3cm to 3.5cm long, 1.5cm wide and 1cm to 2cm deep).
Roughly half of the body of the font has been formed into four facets that are defined by raised ridges on the upper part, opening out into fluting that splays out towards the base of the stone.  There is a lack of consistency in how this was done.  Presumably this was the part of the font that was meant to be seen. The body of the font where the drain hole exists is rounded, so perhaps this side of the font formed the rear.

Situated at the SW end of a narrow steep-sided ridge. Oval platform with a level summit (dims. 20m NNW-SSE; 14m NNE-SSW; H 2.5-4m), separated from the bailey at the SW by a fosse (Wth 3.5m; D 0.8m). The bailey is a level trapezoidal area (max. dims. 32m WNW-ESE; 15m NNE-SSW) defined by an earthen bank (Wth 5-6m; int. H 1m), and an external fosse (max. Wth 5m; D 1m) from SE-W-NW with a further outer bank (max. Wth 5.5m; H 1.7m) at the SW. This fosse, which also encloses the motte along the NE, merges into a berm at the NW and SE along the edges of the ridge. There is a causeway (Wth 2m) across the fosse at the NE extremity. The motte and bailey form one component of a series of earthworks which enclose and divide the ridge summit for a distance of 550m. These include banks along the edge of the ridge, and lateral banks dividing the ridge from NNW-SSE. The most significant are those c. 75m NE of the motte which consist of two banks, 20m apart, cutting the SW end of ridge off from remainder and creating an enclosure around the motte to which three access ramps ascend (from the SW, NW and SE). The SW bank has a central entrance gap (recently widened). A possible moated site (WI020-025----) occurs within the defenses towards the NE. (CUCAP, AIC 86, BGN 24)

Situated on level ground at a break in a S/SW-facing slope. A fifteenth or sixteenth-century nave and chancel parish church (ext. dims. 12m x 6.5m) built of uncoursed masonry with punch-dressed quoins. The W wall has a bellcote and a central door with a possibly later porch. The window in the E wall has glazing-bar-holes and the internal tracery has been removed. Lying on the floor of the church at the W end is a late medieval graveslab (WI021-005003-) (L 1.79m; Wth 0.53-0.74m; T 0.19m) with bevelled edges. The upper face has the outline of a cross at either end joined by a shaft. A second tapering graveslab (WI021-005005-)(min. L 1.06m; Wth at top 0.54m; T 0.28m) stands upright against the outer face of the E wall. The ornament is similar to the former but is more crudely executed. There is no trace of the inscribed granite slab (WI021-005004-) described by Walshe (1931, 139-40). The church stands towards the N side of a rectangular graveyard (WI021-005002-)(dims. 45m NE-SW; 40m NW-SE) defined by a modern stone wall. A motte (WI021-006----) lies 75m to the SW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Situated on level ground at the foot of a steep W-facing slope with gentle slopes to the W and N. The remains consist of the foundations of a tower (ext. dims. 8.6m E-W; 8.5m N-S) constructed of uncoursed rubble (Wth 1.3-1.5m) with a slight base-batter. The S wall is best preserved surviving to a height of 3m at the E end. This wall continues westward possibly representing a bawn (WI021-028001-) to the W of the tower (overall length of S wall 16m) turning northwards at its W end for 3.5m. This N-S section of wall survives as a single course only. Just W of the S wall is a gap (Wth 1.5m) which may represent a doorway with a small segment of wall running E-W (L c. 2m) beyond it. The castle is located on the SE lip of an oval enclosure (WI021-028002-) (int. dims. 44m E-W; 33.5m N-S) defined by a flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 5.8m; D 0.7m). There is no evidence for a causeway or bank but there are traces of an entrance near the possible doorway in the S wall.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Situated on a gentle S-facing slope between the Glendasan and Glenealo rivers. A large quadrangular enclosure (dims. 100m E-W; 110m N-S) defined by a modern wall and stony bank, now surrounds the cathedral, round tower and graveyard at Glendalough. An extension of the wall on the S side of the entrance divides off the N third of the graveyard. This enclosure may be superimposed on an earlier inner enclosure. The overall site is bounded at the N, E and S by rivers and apart from the general outline there is no clear W perimeter. This outer enclosure would have been at least 400m E-W. There is a two-arched gatehouse (WI023-008001-) on the line of the outer enclosure at the NE. (Swan 1985, 95, 98, Fig. 4.16)

Drumgoff Barracks dates from around 1800, and was one of a group of barracks built on the Military Road constructed after the 1798 rising. Not long after it was constructed, Michael Dwyer and the other rebels were captured or surrendered so it had a very short life as a barracks. The other barracks in the group were at Laragh (demolished), Aughavannagh (an An Oige hostel in 1993, present status unknown) and Glencree (now restored by OPW). 19th century crenellated house which replaced 18th century barracks.

Situated on the summit of an E-W ridge with extensive views. Circular area (diam. 50m) on a natural platform defined by an earthen bank (Wth 3-4m; int. H 0.85m; ext. H 2.5m). There is a berm (Wth 4-4.5m) outside the bank from SW-NE, which at the SW merges into a sunken trackway extending W-E along the S perimeter. In the SE quadrant of the interior, backing onto the inside of the bank, is a subtriangular area (dims. 22m NE-SW; 13m NW-SE) defined by a bank and traces of a fosse. Foundations of a rectangular hut (dims. 4.5m x 4m) lie SW of the centre of the enclosure with a subrectangular hollow (dims. 12m x 5m) immediately to the SE. A small triangular annexe (20m E-W; 18m N-S) defined by an earthen bank (Wth 1.5m) is attached to the enclosure at the SE.

The entrance (Wth 1.1m) at the SSE is flanked by radial slabs. In the N sector of the interior, 16m inside the enclosing wall, a circular hut (int. diam. 7m) is defined by a stone wall with inner and outer boulder revetments. There is a standing stone (WI027-043002-) in the centre of the enclosure beside a small stream flowing N-S through the site.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

A well-preserved moated site consisting of a large trapezoidal enclosure (int. dims. 50m E-W; 46m N-S) defined by an earth and stone bank (Wth 1.8-2.2m; max. int. H 1m) with an internal wall-facing (H 0.8m) and an external stone facing in a slight batter to the base of the fosse. The fosse (Wth c. 8m; D 2-2.5m) is steep-sided and flat-bottomed. Situated within a moated site (WI031-002002-) on the summit of a low gently slopped hill with extensive views especially to the S. The remains consist of a vaulted gateway aligned NNE-SSW (L 6.65m; Wth 3.7m), constructed of regular mortared courses with no cut or dressed stone. If symmetric the gateway would have been c. 2.6m wide. Both side-walls are incomplete at the S end, but were probably not much longer. The NW corner is intact but the E wall appears to have continued some distance to the N. A short length of very thick wall (L 1.3m; Wth 1.8m) projects from the E side of the entranceway; there is no indication that this continued further; it may be a buttress or possibly the remains of a perimeter wall. The outer face of the W wall is broken but there is no indication of any adjoining wall on this side. There is no evidence for dating these remains to the 13th century except for the fact that they are sited on a moated site. They may well represent a gateway to a later hall-house or tower house. (O'Flanagan 1928, 120; Price 1936, 47-8)

Situated on an E-facing slope overlooking a stream. A nave (int. dims. 13.3m x 6.6m) and chancel (int. dims. c. 6.6m x 4.8m) church of uncoursed rubble (T 0.8m) surviving to a H of 0.8-1m with a possible doorway at the W end of the S wall. The site is associated with St Baothin and is called Inishboheen; it is probably the site of an Early Christian church. Records suggest that the chancel was added to the earlier nave in the late 1620s (Ronan 1928, 147-8); there is a slight suggestion of the continuation of the nave walls to the E beyond the junction with the chancel. To the W of the church is a rectangular stone block (present H 0.51m; Wth 0.31m; T 0.21m). The only uncut face has the inscription 'RCAC 1690' while the letter 'B' is deeply inscribed on the top. The church is in the NE corner of a subtriangular graveyard (dims. 75m N-S x 50m at N tapering to the S) defined by a modern stone wall. There are several 18th and 19th-century headstones at this site. The church may be the only remains of the medieval borough of Ennisboyne (WI031-020----).

Situated in gently undulating terrain just S of the 18th or early 19th-century Dunganstown House. The lands at Dunganstown were part of the estate of the Hospital of St John of Jerusalem and these were granted in 1597 to Sir John Hoey after the dissolution of the monasteries. The house was probably built in the early 17th century. It consists of a central rectangular block (min. dims. 16.45m E-W; 6.5m N-S) with three storeys and an attic, and Jacobean or Dutch gables. It has two rectangular wings extending from either side to the S (L from façade to S end of the gables 13.4m). A stair tower is attached to the N side of the main block (ext dims. c. 6.43m E-W; 6.25m N-S). There may have been an additional building to the E of this attached to the back of the E wing. The front of the main block is in three bays with a central doorway and a single central window in the gabled attic. No cut stone survives at ground-floor level. Internal features include traces of plaster (probably original) and a fireplace at first-floor level. The attic appears to have been reached by a wooden stairs. The site was apparently damaged in the 1640s and was certainly in ruins in 1655-6 (according to the Down Survey). However, the hood-mouldings over some of the windows may be slightly later, and there are two granite piers to the N of the castle, which may be 18th century in date. There is also a decorated cut stone 'wishing seat' to the S. (Murray 1958, 342)

Situated in gently undulating terrain. Poorly preserved foundations of 'Whaley Abbey' (dims. c. 10.4m E-W; c. 7.7m N-S), a rectangular structure of uncoursed rubble. Recorded by the National Inventory of Architectural Heritage as follows: 
'Detached multiple-bay part one part two part three and part four-storey country house, built 1811 around the fabric of an earlier house. The house is designed part in Romantic Castle style and part in Abbey style. The castle section is articulated with three-stage towers and battlemented parapets while the abbey section is two storey with gothic tracery windows and a battlemented parapet. To the south-east side there is a large conservatory. The building is finished in render with stone dressings. The timber 'studded' and sheeted door has matching sheeting to the blind fanlight and is set within an ogee-shaped opening; this has a reeded stone surround. Window openings are generally flat-headed with gothic tracery and drip mouldings. The house was built in 1811 for LT-Col Robert Howard to designs by Sir Richard Morrison. It is set on a hilltop overlooking the Meeting of the Waters within a large wooded demesne with manicured gardens close to the house. There is a small lake and a boathouse and a tall folly set beside a walled garden.'
(See http://www.buildingsofireland.ie/niah/search.jsp?type=record&county=WI&regno=16403502 [Accessed 21 August 2013])

The only church visible is the present one (built in 1829) which stands outside and to the W of an oval enclosure which surrounds a graveyard (dims. 45m E-W; 30m N-S). The graveyard is raised above the surroundings ground level (H c. 0.8m) and is defined by a slight bank (Wth 2m; max. H 1m) highest at the W. The graveslabs date mainly to the 18th century; the earliest is dated 1712. Among these are a large number of purple slate in the same style as those in Ballymoat (WI024-011001-). Marked 'Church, Grave Yard' on the 1838 OS 6-inch map, although no trace remained of the early church at that time (O'Flanagan 1928, 131).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Situated on a gentle S-facing slope in a small area of scrubby ground with outcropping rock beside a stream (10m W of the tomb). A rectangular chamber (dims. 1.3m x 4.55m) aligned NE-SW, which is largely intact, defined by five sidestones at the N, two to the S, an inset backstone at the E end, and some earthfast boulders. A possible forecourt at the SW end is defined by a vertical slab with the same alignment as the chamber. There is some outer walling on the W side including a small cist-like structure. A raised area (Wth 7.7m; L 7.8m) surrounding the chamber marks the location of the cairn. A single capstone towards the SW entrance survives in situ. Structural stones are of granite and greywacke, and there is a suitable greywacke outcrop 20m to the NE. The tomb is not marked on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. It was investigated by Kinahan in or shortly before 1879, who found a few fragments of charcoal scattered about the gallery and a 'small heap of charcoal' at the E end (Kinahan 1880, 253-7).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Situated on a gentle W-facing slope overlooking a stream (100m to W) on the edge of a pasture field. A nave and chancel church, built of roughly coursed rubble. The chancel (int. dims. c. 3m N-S; c. 5.4m E-W) has well-defined walls. The junction with the less well-preserved nave (int. dims. c. 4m N-S; 8.25m E-W) is obscure but the two portions of the church appear eccentrically aligned. The nave walls are defined by a loose pile of rubble (Wth 1.4-1.8m; av. H 0.3m) and portions of the inner and outer wall facings survive in situ (wall T c. 1.5m). There is no indication of a door or windows. The church is at the E end of an approximately square graveyard enclosure (dims. 52m E-W; 50m N-S) defined on the E and S sides by an earth and stone bank (Wth 2-3.4m; H 0.8-1.2m) with internal drystone walling at the E. At the W the enclosure is defined by a low scarp with a basal revetment of small boulders surviving in patches, while at the N there is a steep scarp flanked by a sunken lane (Wth c. 5m). The E side of the graveyard is reasonably level but it drops away to the W immediately beyond the church.

Situated on a gentle S-facing slope overlooking the valley of the Potters River to the S. While the site is level at the NW it drops markedly to the E and more gently to the S. A nave and chancel church built of roughly coursed rubble. The S side of the nave (dims. 15.4m E-W; 6.85m N-S) is poorly preserved with only a small stretch surviving at the W end. The N wall survives to near full height (H 2.9-3.1m; T 0.85m) with a single break (Wth 2m; H 2m) which may have been the location of a window or door. The W gable also survives to its original height (H 5m) with an opening towards the S end. This has a protruding door portal which may be an original, if unusual, feature. Of the chancel (dims. 4.5m E-W; c. 4.45m N-S) only the N side survives (H 2m). A modern wall divides the nave from the chancel but the two parts appear to be contemporary. There is a granite bullaun stone with an oval basin outside the SW angle of the church. A cylindrical granite font from this site has been removed to the graveyard of St Mary's church at Barndarrig (Ballinacor West townland). The church is situated within a graveyard (dims. c. 60m) which is bounded at the W by the public road and elsewhere by an earth and stone bank (Wth 3m at the NE) which represents the original enclosure. A narrow drainage ditch occurs inside the bank at the N and S while part of the bank at the E has been replaced by a possibly nineteenth-century mortared stone wall (H 1.3m). Outside this is a wide flat-bottomed natural gully (min. Wth 4m). There are two graveslabs dated to 1723 within the church and a substantial number of eighteenth-century headstones in the graveyard.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Situated on a very gentle ENE-facing slope in grassland. In the SW sector of an oval enclosure are several small, uninscribed grave-markers set in rows and a granite cross-slab with pointed head and arms (H 0.94m). The head is broken and lies beside the rest of the cross. One side had a crucifixion figure in low relief which is no longer visible (Price 1945, 257). The enclosure (dims. 45m NE-SW; 30m NW-SE) is defined by an earthen bank, with external drystone facing on the better preserved SW side, (Wth 2.5-3.2m; int. H 0.4-1.2m; ext. H 0.9m) and a shallow external fosse (Wth 2m; D 0.8m) which is not visible at the NE. There are two gaps in the bank; that at the N (Wth 2m) appears to have drystone facing, and that at the S (Wth 1.45m) has bank terminals and a probable causeway over the fosse with a ramp leading up to the interior.

Situated on a gentle N-facing slope with the steep valley of the Aughrim River to the NE. The church lies towards the centre of an oval graveyard (dims. 45.5m N-S; c. 50m E-W) defined by an earth and stone bank (Wth 2-3.8m; int. H 0.6-1m; ext. Situated on level ground between the Redcross River and the sea. A nave (dims. 12m E-W; 5.9m N-S) and chancel (dims. 3.85m E-W; 3.7m N-S) church. The chancel, of roughly coursed slabs, (wall T 1.1m; H 0.8m) is separated from the nave by a narrow opening (Wth 1.2m) in the dividing wall. The nave (wall T 0.7m; max. H 1.35m) is of uncoursed rubble with antae and a possible door at the W. The difference in structural details suggest that the nave was added later. There is a low wall (or buttress) against the inner face of the S wall of the nave. The NW angle and W end of the N wall have collapsed into the church. Situated in the NW sector of an oval enclosure (dims. 40m E-W; 28m N-S) defined by an earth and stone bank (Wth 1.5m) with near vertical outer drystone facing and an entrance at the SE. A granite bullaun stone (dims. 0.38m x 0.29m; T 0.22m) lies on the bank at the S. There is a small slate headstone (dims. 0.88m x 0.33m) inscribed with the words 'JAMES BYRN AND HIS SON...DAUGHTERS DIED IN 1690 S.B.' in the graveyard (at the S end) as well as several early to mid-eighteenth-century headstones. Part of a possible outer enclosure is represented by a shallow fosse (Wth 7m) with an external bank (Wth 2m) and outer fosse (Wth 4m) forming an E-W curve 30m N of the graveyard.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Situated on a level area on a gentle W-facing slope. A Romanesque church (WI042-019001-) stands on the site of a monastery reputed to have been founded in the sixth century. b y St. Finnian of Clonard.   In the graveyard (dims. c. 70m E-W; c. 65m N-S) is St Finden's high cross (WI042-019002-), undecorated except for sunken panels on the sides of the shaft and on the underside of the ring and arms (Harbison 1992, 10). The graveyard contains two fonts (WI042-019009-/010-) (pers. comm Chris Corlett), a possible third font (WI042-019007-) (Graves 1883, 72-6) and a gently tapering, earthfast, granite graveslab with a lightly incised Latin cross on the E face (WI042-019008-). An early wedge-shaped cross-slab (WI042-019006-) previously recorded by Crawford (1925, 66) with a Greek cross in a circle on one side and a human face on the other side was not located recently (pers. comm. C. Corlett, 28 April 2011). An additional 12 cross slabs, two cross bases, a number of architectural fragments and two fragments of a mill stone have recently been identified by C. Corlett (pers. comm. 12 June 2012).  In 1944 the state issued Aghowle National Monument Order No. 8 which prohibited the burial of human remains within and around the area of the Romanesque Church.  
The curvilinear  shape of the graveyard boundary wall probably follows the line of an Early Christian ecclesiastical enclosure (WI042-019004-). Situated 100m to the SE of the site is an earthfast granite bullaun stone with four basins (WI042-019005-).  
(Ordnance Survey Letters Wicklow 1838-40, Corlett and Medleycott eds. 2000, 36-45; Graves 1883, 72-85; Owen 1886, 409; Price 1958, 368-9; Harbison 1970, 251; O'Riordáin 1978, 30, 39, 43, 44)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Situated on the NE edge of a ridge on level ground with a short steep drop to the N and E. According to Price (1946, 90-91) this is an early ecclesiastical church and enclosure (WI043-009003-). A ruined early nineteenth-century structure with no surviving evidence of an earlier church. A cylindrical block of granite mentioned by Price (1946, 90) lies just outside the SW corner of the church and there are some other miscellaneous architectural fragments. The graveyard contains a large number of mid-eighteenth-century headstones. The church and graveyard lie just S of the centre of a large oval enclosure (dims. 100m N-S; c. 65m E-W) defined at the E and W by an earthen bank (Wth 3m; H 2m) with drystone facing. No indication of a fosse. There may have been an entrance at the NW where the enclosure is approached by a raised path between two ditches.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

It has no inscription or decoration on it, just plain stone’ (OPW file 1964). This record records the original location of the font at a burial ground (WI046-003----). The font has since been moved and its present location is unknown.

Situated on level ground with a gentle slope and extensive views to the S. A substantial 16th-century tower house now incorporated into a late 18th/early 19th-century Georgian Gothic house. The tower house consists of the main four-storey tower and a large adjoining angle tower with a turret, which forms one angle of the present building. The modern entrance, in the angle between the tower house and angle tower, is the original doorway into the original building itself, through a two-centred granite arch. There is another turret on the tower house at the NW corner. To the N of the entrance at second-floor level is a machicolation, while garderobe chutes are visible in the external face of the tower on the opposite side. It is still occupied.

Described by the National Inventory of Architectural Heritage as follows:

'Detached multiple-bay two storey former pair of houses, the most northerly of which was built c.1675, now in use as one dwelling. Flanking the houses are two farm buildings which give the grouping a 'U'-plan. The timber sheeted door is set within a flat-headed opening. Window openings are also flat-headed with a mixture of two over two timber sash frames and replacement top-hung frames. The pitched roofs are finished with natural slate and cast-iron rainwater goods. The southern section has a dentilled eaves course. Chimneystacks are of varying size; all are rendered and have no pots. Internally there are three very large chimney breasts which contain inglenooks. One contains the remains of a bread oven. The house is set on a slight rise within its own grounds.'

Situated on a gentle N-facing slope. Historical references to 'Derrylossary church' which was granted to the prebend of the Chancellor of St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin, by the archbishop of Dublin, have been identified with this site (Ronan 1928, 134). A modern church and walled graveyard now occupy the site and there is no trace of the original church. The site is encompassed by the remains of an oval bivallate enclosure (int. diam. c. 100m; ext. diam. c. 150m) best preserved at the N. The inner bank is incorporated in the N wall of the graveyard and from there curves SW towards the road. The outer bank (Wth 3m; H 0.3m) and external fosse (Wth 4.8; D 0.5m) are also in evidence only at the N. There are three granite bullaun stones within the enclosure, one inside and one outside the W wall of the graveyard and one 15m NE of the graveyard wall. Price and Stephens (1948, 179) also describe a fourth c. 200m NW of church (ibid., 130-31) which was located by Chris Corlett in 2005 (see WI018-012----).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Situated on a gentle S-facing slope overlooking the valley of the Potters River to the S. While the site is level at the NW it drops markedly to the E and more gently to the S. A nave and chancel church built of roughly coursed rubble. The S side of the nave (dims. 15.4m E-W; 6.85m N-S) is poorly preserved with only a small stretch surviving at the W end. The N wall survives to near full height (H 2.9-3.1m; T 0.85m) with a single break (Wth 2m; H 2m) which may have been the location of a window or door. The W gable also survives to its original height (H 5m) with an opening towards the S end. This has a protruding door portal which may be an original, if unusual, feature. Of the chancel (dims. 4.5m E-W; c. 4.45m N-S) only the N side survives (H 2m). A modern wall divides the nave from the chancel but the two parts appear to be contemporary. There is a granite bullaun stone with an oval basin outside the SW angle of the church. A cylindrical granite font from this site has been removed to the graveyard of St Mary's church at Barndarrig (Ballinacor West townland). The church is situated within a graveyard (dims. c. 60m) which is bounded at the W by the public road and elsewhere by an earth and stone bank (Wth 3m at the NE) which represents the original enclosure. A narrow drainage ditch occurs inside the bank at the N and S while part of the bank at the E has been replaced by a possibly nineteenth-century mortared stone wall (H 1.3m). Outside this is a wide flat-bottomed natural gully (min. Wth 4m). There are two graveslabs dated to 1723 within the church and a substantial number of eighteenth-century headstones in the graveyard.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wicklow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1997). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

Situated on the NE edge of a ridge on level ground with a short steep drop to the N and E. According to Price (1946, 90-91) this is an early ecclesiastical church (WI043-009001-) and enclosure (WI043-009003-). An architectural fragment, described as a lozenge-shaped trough (dims. c. 0.4m x 0.2m; D 0.2m), may be a stoup (D of depression c. 0.08m). Test-trenching under licence no. 99E0302 was undertaken at a house site as part of the requirements of Wicklow County Council for granting planning permission for construction of a dwelling. The site is beside an ecclesiastical enclosure that contains the ruins of a church and 18th-century graveyard at Ballymaghroe, Ashford, Co. Wicklow.
The ground slopes gradually down to the southern end of the site, where the proposed house is to be built. A tracking machine with a 2m-wide flat bucket was used to strip the soil to a depth of 0.2m for half the width and for the full length of the driveway, west of the graveyard. A new entrance driveway to an existing house north of the graveyard was similarly de-sodded, and a wall trench was dug to accommodate a wider entrance.
Test-trenching was carried out around the original location of the proposed house, in the percolation area and on the site of the septic tank. Trenches were dug to the depth of the undistributed subsoil where the outside-wall trenches were to be dug. The south-east trench (1) revealed a 4m-long, 0.2m-deep layer of charcoal-rich soil below the topsoil, which contained evidence of ironworking. The feature extended northward (Trench 5) to cover an area of at least 4m diameter. A second, similar feature was exposed to the north of this area.
It was agreed with the owner that a parallel set of house trenches be tested 15m south of the original position in order to avoid the necessity to excavate the feature.
No other archaeological features were recorded.

The development site lies at the corner of Church Street and Wentworth Place, Wicklow, and is within the zone of archaeological potential for the town. Recent excavations by James Eogan in an adjoining property (Excavations 1997, 202, 97E0118) identified a series of medieval pits and two shallow ditches.  Test-trenching was carried out by Una Cosgrave and involved the mechanical excavation of two trenches (No. 698 above). Limited archaeological deposits consisting of a light brown, fine, sandy clay with occasional charcoal flecking were recorded in both trenches. No datable material was recovered from this layer.   Given the identification of potentially significant deposits revealed during the test-trenching programme, Dúchas The Heritage Service recommended the archaeological monitoring of all further subsurface works. 
Monitoring took place over two days and revealed the same formation processes of modern rubble and gravels sealing rubble layers containing red brick as identified in the test-trenching programme. The potentially archaeologically significant clay with occasional charcoal flecking was revealed in the north-eastern corner of the site. However, as excavation for foundation trenches only proceeded to a depth of c. 0.65m in this area, only the top 50mm of this layer was exposed. As this layer was only revealed in a 1m-long east-west foundation trench, it was not possible to define fully its extent, character and condition. There would be no further disturbance caused to this layer by the development. No datable material was recovered, and no further archaeological features or finds were revealed.

In late October 1990, the remains of two skeletons were discovered during site clearance for a development of 16 new houses on high ground to the west of, and overlooking, Wicklow town. As a result, a number of test trenches were opened in order to delimit the extent of the burials, together with any other archaeological features occurring on the site. Each of the test trenches was 0.7m wide and varied in length from c. 3m-34m.
A further five skeletons were uncovered, each one orientated east-west, fully extended with their heads lying to the west. In four of the five cases, the skeletons were dug into a sterile yellow clay and were consequently in a poor state of preservation, with only traces of their lower body bones being visible. No finds were recovered within these deposits. Overlying this yellow clay, a stony gravel deposit was laid, into which a single extended skeleton, in an excellent state of preservation, was uncovered. A number of sherds of Leinster cooking ware were retrieved from this deposit.
In one of the trenches, a mortar-bonded stone feature was exposed, set into the clay deposit to the east, and the gravel deposit to the west. About 0.7m wide, it extended north-south for a distance of c. 0.8m, turned to the east, where a clean face could be identified, and extended for a further length of c. 0.5m. It did not extend into any of the adjacent test trenches. A number of sherds of medieval pottery were recovered from the gravel deposit abutting this feature to the west.
Further to the north a number of shallow stone features were identified, set into the dense yellow clay, with no evidence for mortar bonding. They consisted of one course of stones and were 0.4m-0.45m wide with a maximum identified length of c. 3.5m.
Further to the north and east of the burial area, a number of test trenches, orientated east-west, were dug down to bedrock, which occurred 0.3m-0.7m below present ground surface. A number of north-south cuts were noted in the bedrock. About 0.8m-1.1m in width 0.08m-0.3m in depth and continuing downslope in a northerly direction, their full extent remains undetermined due to the trial trenching being terminated before they were fully exposed. They were filled with dry loam and charcoal, within which a number of sherds of Leinster cooking ware were recovered. In one of these features a partially damaged medieval relief tile was embedded into the loam fill. The design on the tile is quite distinct, albeit incomplete; a horse with rider, bridle piece and reins, two birds, and possibly a deer with antlers can be identified. Traces of a green glaze can also be seen.
The site has not yet been fully archaeologically resolved. A full excavation of the burial area may take place some time in the future, or alternatively, an area of open space may be located over the burials, thus leaving them undisturbed. Trial trenching was funded by the developer (Bennett 1990)

Gentle SE facing slope of grazing land. Fine views towards Wicklow Head and out to sea. A large oblong cairn 17m NW-SE x 9m NE-SW, 1.7m high at NW and SE ends, 2.1m high elsewhere. The SW side of the cairn has been clearly dug away, and this is confirmed by local information that stones were drawn from the site for surfacing local lanes. It is likely therefore that the cairn was more circular than is presently the case. 
While in some ways the cairn appears to simply represent a large clearance cairn, given its scale, and the fact that it has been partially quarried away, and also given the lack of any further such clearance cairns in any neighbouring fields, it seems most likely that this is a prehistoric burial cairn.

Excavations under licence no. 02E0329 took place at Inchanappa Upper from 13 March until 24 April 2002. During this time 32 postholes, stake-holes or post sockets, eight burnt pit features, seven unburned pit features, two field boundary ditches, two ditches of unknown function, one trench feature, one natural depression and one recent cable trench were excavated.
In the West Area there were two post-holes and four to five features that are the probable windbreak elements. In the Central Area there were two burnt pit features with post-holes in association, one isolated burnt pit feature and one area of oxidised earth that is spatially associated with a short trench. The North Area had no post-holes associated with the lone burnt pit feature. Also in this area was an oval pit feature with a small area of burnt shale. The central feature in the East Area of the site consisted of a probable corn-drying kiln that appears to have been attached to, or partially enclosed within, a hut structure (www.excavations.ie).

National Monument in state ownership No. 449.  The 'Dwyer-McAllister Cottage' is a fine example of a traditional thatched cottage built with local stone and whitewashed inside and out. It was from this cottage, in the Winter of 1799, that the famed rebel, Michael Dwyer, fought the encircling British groups and finally made good his escape over the snow covered mountains. The cottage was later destroyed by fire and lay in ruins for almost 150 years. It was restored to its original form as a monument in the late 1940's and again extensively repaired and re-roofed in 1992. It is a National Monument in State care (No. 449).

On a gentle SW-facing, lower slope of Sorrell Hill, overlooking a valley formed by Black Hill to the S. In an area of open mountain grazing outside modernly enclosed land. A complex of six hut sites (WI010-059001- to WI010-059005- and WI010-059008-), clearance cairns (WI010-059006-) and field boundary walls (WI010-059007-) lies within a relatively small and well-defined area, bounded by a small stream at the SE, and at the NW by a NE-SW field boundary, which is probably 19th century in date. At the SE end of the group an L-shaped stone wall is probably the remains of a modern sheep pen. Otherwise, the hut sites, clearance cairns and stone walls appear to be contemporary, and are likely to represent booleying or transhumance of an early date, perhaps during the Early Christian period. The hut sites are scattered in a roughly linear fashion along the edge of a well-defined scarp, where the ground falls away into boggy, wet ground. Hut site A (WI010-059001-), the most south easterly of the hut sites, is defined by a low setting of stones (int. diam. 2.2m) and appears to be cut into the natural slope at the N and NE. There is a possible entrance at S (Wth 0.4m). Another hut site (WI010-059008-) lies 1.6m to the N.

The font presently held in the disused RC church at Knockananna came from Ballymaghroe Graveyard (WI033-009001-) having been moved from there sometime before 1933 (Corlett & Weaver 2002, vol. 1, 188). It consists of a large, cylindrical block of granite (diam. 0.68m; H 0.56m), the upper edge of which is damaged, containing a roughly circular basin (diam. 0.48m; D 0.21m) with a drain hole (diam. 0.035m) which exits the side of the font from where a linear groove (Wth 0.035m; D 0.05m) extends down the side of the stone (L 0.14m). On the outer edge of the font are two opposing crosses, both carved in low relief. One (dims. H 0.46m; Wth 0.19m) is formed by a low (H 0.02m; Wth 0.05-0.08m) raised band. The top of the second cross is missing (H 0.3m; Wth 0.18m), where the top of the font has been damaged. It is similarly defined by a low raised band (H 0.015m; Wth 0.06-0.08m).

The stone marks the entrance to a housing estate, and has the estate's name 'Coves Brook' and the year '1999' carved on one side. There are a number of large granite boulders placed in various points in the green areas of this estate, and it seems most likely that they were all found during the construction of the estate. Therefore, the rock art itself may have come from quite close to its present location. The general aspect here is of a S-facing slope with good commanding views S, towards Slieveboy in Co. Wexford. The granite boulder (dims. L 1.6m; Wth 1m; T 0.8m) is now placed on its edge, with the decorated side now on a vertical face, but originally the stone was most likely positioned so that the decoration occurred on the upper horizontal surface of the stone. The stone was probably formerly earthfast, and plough marks that score the edge of the decorated surface suggest that only a small portion of the boulder originally protruded above the ground surface. Most of the decoration occurs on a relatively flat face. There are two double ring and cup motifs (cup diams. 5cms; D 1.5 - 2cm; enclosing rings ext. diams 12cm and 18cm). There is another cup with traces of a ring (ext. diam. 20cm across) but it is unclear if there is also an inner circle in this case. There are also some six cup marks scattered across this face, while the surface of the stone rises above the flat surface at one side, and there are two further cups on this ridge. (The unknown original location of this monument is designated WI047-018001-.)

Not indicated on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps, but clearly visible on recent OSi aerial photographs, and marked on the most recent OS ITM map. Leinster, as well as Kilranelagh Hill nearby to the W, and NW towards Brusselstown and Spinans Hill. The site is intervisible with the large enclosure at Keadeen to the north (WI027-43----) and 'Crossoona Rath' in Boleycarrigeen (WI027-038----). While the area around the enclosure is overgrown with gorse, the interior is grassy and generally gorse-free, however, gorse does obscure some of the enclosing bank/wall. An oval area (diams. c.70m E-W; 53m N-S) is defined by an earth and stone bank at the N (Wth. 2.8m; H 0.5m), which has been largely robbed out along the E where material may have been used in the construction of the nearby stone wall. At S and SW the enclosing element takes the form of a collapsed stone wall (Wth 2.2m; H 0.4m). The entrance appears to be at the S, where two stones (H 0.70m and 0.85m) set on edge (with a third loosely jambed between them) appear to define the W side of the entrance. The E side is overgrown with gorse, but 2.8m E of these stones another large stone may define the eastern side of the entrance. A a small circular hut site (WI027-087001-) lies to SE of centre within the enclosure.

Situated on a N-facing slope within a copse of conifers c. 9m up-slope from a farm track. The remains consist of a chamber-like feature defined by two orthostats on the N and two other possible orthostats on the S. The ‘chamber’ is orientated WSW – ENE and is wedge-shaped in plan with the wider element (1.55m at E) narrowing to 0.85m at W. The E of the two uprights forming the S side measures 1.9m long, 0.35m thick and stands 0.7m high. It is separated by 0.6m from its W counterpart which measure 2.3m long, 0.3m thick and is 1m high. These stones give an overall ‘chamber’ length of 4.85m. There are three wedge-indentations or marks visible on the upper interior edge of the E stone and a single example is visible on the W end of the W orthostat. These are V-shaped in profile with a rounded point at the bottom. The edges of these marks are not sharp and they do not appear to have been made using metal tools. The two stones that form the possible S side lean markedly inwards to the N and it is unclear if both were ever fully erect: no wedge-marks are visible on these stones. The E stone measures 1.4m long, is at least 0.2m thick and, if erect, would have been at least 0.6m high. The slab beside it to the W measures 1.85m long, 0.3m thick and, if erect, would have been 0.8m high: its top rests against a tree growing in the ‘chamber’. Some 2m W of this stone is a low orthostat set transversely to the line of the so-called ‘chamber’ sides. It measures 0.7m long, 0.27m thick and is 0.25m high: its function and relationship to the others is unclear. The area within the ‘chamber’ is lower than the surrounding ground and it is possible that it has been dug out. There is a small spoil heap immediately to the N and just outside the junction of the two N orthostats and the raised area immediately E of the ‘chamber’ may also be the result of digging. There are other stones apparently set or raised in similar positions on the hillside within the copse and it is impossible to be certain which are natural features and which may be the result of quarrying operations. The ‘chamber’ remains cannot be classified with certainty in their present condition, and while the monument shares certain affinities with those of the megalithic tomb class, especially wedge tombs, the evidence is not sufficient to warrant accepting it as a genuine example.

It consists of an uprooted granite boulder, to the rear of a derelict farmhouse. The fields here have been cleared and improved in relatively recent years and it is likely that the boulder was moved to its present position from a location nearby, most likely from the north where the ground rises. The location comprises a south facing slope of a ridge. To the east there is a view of the Ballyduff Pass, whereas the views of the mountains to the south and southwest are blocked by the mature trees that surround the adjacent farmhouse. This large boulder measures 1.9m x 1.6m (max) across, and 1.3m high. It is clear that this was originally an earthfast boulder whereby the majority of the stone was buried below the surface. One end of the top surface of the stone is undecorated, which may indicate that this portion of the stone never protruded above the ground surface. Instead, the decoration is concentrated on the remaining two-thirds of the upper surface and comprises a dense collection of at least 40 shallow cup marks averaging 3cm to 4cm across. Many of the cups appear to be arranged in pairs and in one or two instances are conjoined. Roughly central within decorated area is a shallow borehole, which may indicate an abortive attempt to split the stone in modern times. The cup marks have been quite significantly weathered, but there are no obvious traces of rings that once enclosed any of the cup marks, and given the density of the decoration, it is possible that none of the cup marks were originally enclosed. At corner is a triangular formation of quartz veins, and within the triangular space appear to be traces of 5 cup marks and a short groove.

WI018-053----_01.jpg and WI018-053----_02.jpg show the rock art on the boulder (Photographs: Christiaan Corlett).

This granite boulder was dug up during the construction of a house around 2008 and was retained as a garden feature adjacent to the entrance gate. This is a relatively level site, whereby the views are presently obstructed by vegetation and buildings, but formerly there would have been a commanding view of Djouce to the north.  The granite boulder measures 1.7m x 1.32m across and stands 75cm high. Given the presence of plough marks along two edges of the stone it is clear that it was formerly an earthfast boulder, whereby the decorated face was situated relatively close to the surface. The decorated surface is slightly domed and features a vein of quartz extending diagonally across the top. The surface is also very weathered so that the decoration is quite poorly preserved. There are five large cupmarks ranging from 4cm to 6cm across and 1.5cm deep. There are faint traces of circles enclosing at least three of these larger cupmarks. There are also traces of 12 smaller and shallower cup marks.

WI018-054----_01.jpg and WI018-054----_02.jpg show the rock art on the boulder (Photographs: Christiaan Corlett).

Site described by Dr. Clíodhna Ní Lionáin of the UCD Wicklow Rock Art Project as following; 'Located close to a field wall, to the east of the farm house. There are a number of other stones here, including a small sub-circular stone with a large cupmark and a number of fragmentary disc querns.  A small, sub-rectangular (dims. 0.69m x 0.28m x 0.19m thick) granite stone, with some moss growth. It is no longer in its original location.Only one face is decorated. The art consists of a combination of cup-and-ring motifs, linear grooves, and cupmarks. The two cup-and-ring motifs, which are joined by a linear connector (23cm long), consist of a cupmark (3-4cm diameter) enclosed by a single ring (overall motif size: 8cm, 10cm). There are two cupmarks to the right (3cm diam.) of and above (4cm diam.) the smaller cup-and-ring motif. Linear grooves extend from each of these cupmarks – a 30cm groove from the smaller cupmark, and a 13cm groove from the larger cupmark. Another groove (19cm long) is located to the left of the larger cup-and-ring motif and appears to follow the outline of the stone. There are a further three possible cupmarks above the linear groove that links the two cup-and-ring motifs'(www.wicklowrockartproject.com).

National Monument in state guardianship No. 416.  A large domed cupmarked granite boulder (dims. 2.4m x 2m x H 1.4m) known locally as the 'Piper Stone' stands c. 40m NE of stone circle (WI015-010----) depicted on the OS 6-inch map as 'The Pipers Stones'.  The upper surface of the boulder features a cross shaped groove (dims. Wth 0.06-0.1m x 0.03-0.05m D).  One of the grooves is aligned E-W and follows a vein of quartz.  The second groove is roughly N-S.  North of the intersection the groove is well-defined.  However, south of the intersection the groove is very shallow, and extends down the side of the slab, whereas elsewhere the grooves are restricted to the upper surface of the boulder. Six cup marks can also be found on the upper surface of the boulder. Three cupmarks (max. diam. 0.17m x 0.03m D) are found in the NW quadrant formed by the cross.  A single cupmark (diam. 0.10m x 0.02m D) occurs in the NE quadrant. There are two further cupmarks in the SE quadrant (diam. 0.11m x 0.02m deep). There are no cupmarks evident in the SW quadrant.

Located at what was a N-facing slope overlooking the valley of the River Liffey before it was flooded and turned into the Pollaphuca reservoir. The reduced water level has revealed archaeological features on the newly exposed ground. 
The granite stone is D-shaped in plan with two straight edges (L 42cm and 23cm), although it has a maximum ‘width’ of 40cm, almost as great as its long side. The height varies from 14cm to 22 cm and it has probably been shaped into its present form, which would just about contain one basin when completed. The underside is generally rounded but it has a skelp removed which was probably accidental and accounts for the different height of the stone at different sides. The upper surface has a single basin (diam. 19cm x 20cm; max. D 4cm). The peck marks used to excavate the basin can be seen clearly, so the bullaun stone was never finished and used as otherwise the surface of the basin would have been ground smooth.

Located at what was a N-facing slope overlooking the valley of the River Liffey before it was flooded and turned into the Pollaphuca reservoir. The standing stone is just on the NW side (by c. 1-2m) of a relict field bank extending off to the NE and visible now as the stumps of bushes. This field bank is marked on the Cassini OS map. The standing stone is on a point jutting out into the reservoir at the moment, and this would agree with the contours on the Cassini map suggesting it is a low spur. There is a wide view out from W-N-E and three passage tombs on top of mountains to the E are within view.
The shore is very steep here and even though the standing stone is only about 3m out from firm ground a black silt has accumulated between the stone and shore. The mud makes it impossible to get near the stone but the firm ground can be felt 45cm below its surface. The visible height above the mud is 85cm and it comes to a point. The stone is probably granite and at the mud surface it has a rectangular cross-section 35cm x 25cm with the long axis aligned 290 degrees (magnetic). It has a total height above the subsoil of 1.3m. The stone leans a little to the N and its point is over the N side.

Located at what was probably the crest of an E-facing slope overlooking the valley of the River Liffey before it was flooded and turned into the Pollaphuca reservoir. From the Cassini edition of the OS map the location is close to a steep cliff down to the Liffey. The water of the reservoir has eroded away the topsoil and a lot of the subsoil on a fairly level plateau. Judging by the little cliff around the normal edge of the full reservoir about 30-40cm of subsoil has been removed at the edge of the shore where wave action would perhaps erode more of the soil, but the topsoil and some amount of subsoil has been removed from the extensive ground exposed now at the SE edge of Burgage More townland. The cursus (WI005-124----) is in full view at the top of a hill to the E.  
After consultation with Pauline Gleeson and Sean Kirwan of the NMS it was decided to excavate the two pits. The subsoil is hard yellow clay and when it is cleaned back the pits are visible as softer brown soil with plentiful amounts of charcoal and burnt bone visible as white flecks. The white fecks are not to be confused with the white flecks of bird droppings which are also present. The first pit identified and excavated was oval (dims 23cm x 18cm; D 10cm) and its entire contents were removed for sieving.  No pottery was present that we could see but it contained a soft brown soil and charcoal. The second, western, pit was smaller (dims 20cm x 18cm; D 5cm) and much less soil was recovered from it, but bone and charcoal was present.

The ditch is between 26cm and 35cm wide. There is a break in the ditch (Wth 0.5m) at NW, and where the furrow runs over the monument and crosses the ditch at SW and NE the ditch could not be made out, particularly at NE where there is a gap of 1.75m. The gap at NW is too small to be an official opening, and is probably where the ditch is so shallow that it has eroded away. The gap at NE is too wide to be that of a hut-site so the feature is probably a barrow. 
Three small pits were identified in the interior, although none was at the centre. The pits have diameters of 20-25cm and are widely spaced in relation to each other but within 1m of the ditch. They contain charcoal and are probably the bases of cremation burials rather than post-holes.

In 2010 an archaeological assessment, including geophysical survey (licence 10R0008) and testing, was undertaken by Irish Archaeological  Consultancy Ltd. in advance of the construction of a distribution road at IDA Lands, Killincarrig, Greystones, Co. Wicklow. Test-trenching under licence No. 10E0025 took place from 26 January 2010, using a 20-tonne mechanical excavator equipped with a flat, toothless bucket. A total of 23 test-trenches (totalling 603 linear metres) were excavated across the proposed development area. The development area is currently formed by a large greenfield area located to the immediate east of the recently constructed Greystones relief road (R762).
The archaeology uncovered on-site was all located on the higher ground where the ground level slopes away to the north and east. The remains on-site were spread over an area measuring 55m east–west by 25m. The archaeological features appeared to be clustered in two areas along the east–west-orientated section of the proposed road. The nature of the features (i.e. possible pits, post-holes, stake-holes and hearths) suggests that they represent the remains of a habitation site. The shallow nature of the features and the presence of several plough furrows indicate that the features have been heavily truncated by agricultural activity.
The pottery uncovered from one of the features suggests a prehistoric date for the site. It is very possible that remains continue outside of the route corridor to the north and may form a part of the Bronze Age site excavated between 90m and 125m to the north-north-east (WI013–086 and WI013–085).
Nothing of archaeological significance was noted in the north–south section of the proposed road. The geophysical survey suggested the presence of a substantial linear feature within this area, along with a number of potential archaeological features and trends, but nothing of archaeological significance was identified during testing. This would suggest that natural geology such as sand, gravel and stones, which were apparent within the subsoil through the testing exercise, were responsible for these anomalies.  The site was excavated in March 2010 by Yvonne Whitty under the same licence number (www.excavations.ie).
The results of this excavation were summarised as following;'Excavation at Killincarrig, Greystones was carried out in advance of the construction of a distributor road for an IDA business park. Three phases of fieldwork took place between 22 February and 27 May 2010.   Three phases of activity were identified at Killincarrig.  The focus of the early Neolithic activity was a structure at the northern limits of the excavation made up of a foundation slot-trench, seven post-holes and ten stake-holes. It is believed that more of this structure lies outside of the area of excavation to the north. The exact form of this structure is unclear.
Another group of post-holes was excavated to the west of this structure. These appear to have been part of a further structure but again its form is unclear and further features may still lie outside of the area of excavation to the north. It is believed to be early Neolithic due to its proximity to the other structure, although none of the post-holes contained any dating evidence and the construction style appears to be very different, with no foundation trench present. The structures are believed to have been houses due to the high quantity of features containing domestic material found to the south of them.
These features were made up of pits and post-holes. The post-holes did not appear to have been part of a structure. The purpose of the pits is unclear. Further features were excavated at the east of the site, including pits, post-holes, a stake-hole, a hearth and a number of spreads. Although some of these features are thought to be related to one another due to their proximity, their purpose is unclear. They are thought to be a result of domestic activity related to the structures. Early Neolithic pottery and flints were found in many of these features and so all are considered to be from this period. Two further early Neolithic pits were excavated at the south-west of the site. One appeared to have held a post at its northern end. It is unclear what phase of activity three further features to the north of these features were from.   A single early/middle Bronze Age pit was excavated at the north of Area A between the two structures outlined above. Other features in the area may also be early/middle Bronze Age in date, but it is unclear which, if any, are.
A single late Iron Age/early medieval hearth was excavated towards the south-west of Area A. Three features near to this hearth, including another hearth, may be related, although they may also be related to the early Neolithic activity recorded around the site.   Further undated features, including a hearth, pits, post-holes and stake-holes, were excavated in Area B. The hearth had post- and stake-holes at its north-east and south-west sides and appeared to have been used for cooking or other domestic activities.  Additional testing was carried out by Fintan Walsh beyond the wayleave of the proposed road in order to assess the extent of the archaeological features' (www.excavations.ie). 
Additional test-trenching was undertaken in advance of the construction of a distribution road at IDA Lands, Killincarrig, Greystones, Co. Wicklow. This additional phase of testing, which involved the excavation of six strategically placed test-trenches on either side of the area of excavation (within the footprint of the road), was undertaken to access the extent of archaeological deposits/features within the lands made available.  Test-trenching took place on 28 April 2010, using a 13-tonne mechanical excavator equipped with a flat, toothless bucket. This phase of testing identified a concentration of archaeological features, similar to that identified and excavated within the excavation area, which were identified on the northern end of the excavation area and extend up to the limit of the lands made available. There were a number of features at the western end of the scheme, suggesting a concentration of archaeological activity in this area. These are likely to be similar in nature to those identified in the excavation area (charcoal-rich features with lithics and pottery). A small number of features at the western end of the scheme, to the south of the excavation area, may also indicate archaeological activity extending in this direction correlating with the increased occurrence of activity in this area indicated in the excavation area.

Situated on E bank of stream which marks townland boundary with Bullford, mill race located to W.  Three distinct areas of burnt spread material in close proximity were identified during the digging of an electricity services trench in an area on the western boundary of a housing development site. Ditch-barrow in area 4A was excavated in 2020 under licence 17E0292 by Muireann Ní Cheallacháin for IAC Archaeology during construction phase of residential development by Cairn Homes PLC.  
Monument was described as following; 'Ring-ditch was annular in plan with a 3.5m internal diameter and a depth of only 0.2m. The shallow nature of the ring ditch is possibly indicative of modern truncation though ploughing. C3 contained a main silty sand fill (C4) present throughout
the length of the feature along with four primary charcoal deposits recorded along the base
(C25, C37, C41 & C43). These primary deposits did not appear to contain any burnt bone inclusions. Two middle charcoal deposits (C6 & C21) did not appear to contain burnt bone either. Three definite discrete cremation deposits (C5, C10 and C42) containing frequent charcoal and moderate burnt bone inclusions were recorded directly above the main fill (C4). A possible heat affected flint chunk was retrieved from cremation deposit C42.  The cremation deposits were all shallow in nature which suggests they were deposited on the backfilled barrow ditch and were not contained in individual cremation pits.  A small shallow circular pit (C30) was recorded less than 1m to the east of the ring barrow and it contained a single silty sand fill with moderate charcoal inclusions. The function of pit C30 may be associated in some form with the ring barrow (C3), however no other features were recorded in the periphery of the ring barrow' (Ní Cheallacháin and Spencer 2020, 36-7).

Recently discovered in a graveyard (WI015-035002-). Three disarticulated carved stone fragments which are likely to be from a single cross: portion of a cross-shaft, a cross-head and a possible cross-base.

A gently splaying, granite, cross shaft fragment, which includes its base, is loosely earthfast and was likely reused as a grave marker (L 52cm; Wth 21cm; T 12cm at base; T 14cm at top). The surviving upper end shows a relatively clean break and the angles of the shaft are slightly rounded. Both sides and one face are plain, while on the opposite face there is a central, linear band (L 31cm; Wth 4cm) which is slightly raised (H 0.5 to 0.8cm) proud of the face. This band stops abruptly at a horizontal ledge that punctuates the bottom of the shaft which would have been inserted in a socket. This portion of the face has been reduced by about 1cm but this reduction does not extend around the sides or across the opposite face. 

See attached image: WI015-035003-_1 C. Corlett 11-10-2022

A granite cross head (Wth 52cm; H 42cm; T 14cm) rests on the ground surface. Just below the arms, there is a relatively clean break across the shaft, the dimensions of which (Wth 21.5cm; T 14cm) closely match those of the shaft fragment described above. A low, circular bosse (H 1cm; diam. 7cm) is carved between the cross arms and there appears to be a raised ridge extending vertically below the bosse, but it is quite weathered and poorly defined. On the opposite face, the crudely incised letters ‘gD’ are carved in the upper arm and the year ‘1712’ across the transverse arms (with a gap between ‘17’ and ‘12’ at the centre of the cross arms). This carving is clearly secondary and probably indicates reuse as a grave marked at the beginning of the 18th century. 

See attached images: WI015-035003-_2 and WI015-035003-_3 C. Corlett 11-10-2022

A possible cross base survives as a badly damaged, partly earthfast, rectangular granite block (L 50cm; Wth 26cm; H 33cm). Only one side along with a short return of one end of the socket (D 23cm) it contains survives. While the opposite end is missing, a scar-line where the side has broken away suggests that the socket was c. 21cm in width. The surviving socket-side is straight-sided and the bottom of the socket is flat suggesting it is the remains of a cross base. There is no trace of decoration on the external sides, which are quite rounded and only crudely shaped. 

See attached images: WI015-035003-_4 and WI015-035003-_5 C. Corlett 11-10-2022

A Geophysical Survey (Detection Device Licence no. 22R0231) was carried out in relation to Wicklow County Council Planning Ref. 22/544 regarding a proposed residential development in Newcastle, Co. Wicklow.
The survey revealed two previously unidentified monuments in level pasture, both clearly defined and interpreted as ring ditches, located c. 20m apart. Their existence was subsequently confirmed during archaeological test trenching (Excavation Licence no. 22E0502).
The larger ringditch (WI019-081----) was a circular area (int. diam. c. 10m) enclosed by a ditch (av. Wth 1.7m; av. D 0.82m) and is to be preserved in situ.
The smaller one (WI019-082----) lies c. 20m to the NE and is also circular (int. diam. c. 5m; ext. dia. c. 7m) and has a possible entrance at east-southeast. It is to be preserved by record.
